blocks.html: In Living or Not Living? you learned that living things grow, need food and water, and make more of their kind. Scientists use a fuller list. A thing is alive only if it shows all of these signs together.

Every living thing (1) is made of one or more cells, (2) uses energy, (3) grows and develops, (4) responds to its surroundings, (5) keeps its insides steady (homeostasis), and (6) produces offspring that inherit its traits.

blocks.name: bi-classify

cards.why: A crystal grows, but it is not made of cells and uses no energy of its own.
A mushroom is made of cells, feeds on wood and makes spores.
Fire uses fuel and gives off energy, but it has no cells and no offspring.
A seed is alive and resting: its cells use a little energy until it sprouts.
A robot responds to its surroundings, but it is not made of cells and cannot grow.

opts.prompt: Sort each card. Tap a card, then a group.

blocks.cap: Sort the tricky cases: each one shows at least one sign of life.

blocks.html: Many nonliving things show one sign. A crystal grows. A fire uses energy and spreads. A robot responds. But none of them is made of cells, and none produces offspring that inherit its traits. Only living things show the whole set, which is why scientists test for all six.

blocks.title: A seed in a packet
blocks.q: A bean seed has sat in a dry packet for a year. Is it alive?
steps: Is it made of cells? Yes: a seed holds a tiny plant made of cells.
Does it use energy? Yes, slowly, while it rests.
Can it grow, respond and make offspring? Given water, it sprouts, grows toward light, and later makes seeds of its own.
blocks.a: Yes. It is alive, only resting.

blocks.title: Which sign is it?
blocks.q: You shiver on a cold day, and your body warms up. Which characteristic is that?
steps: Shivering is a response, but its purpose is to hold your body temperature steady.
Keeping conditions inside the body steady is homeostasis.

blocks.html: Judging by one sign, often movement or growth. A car moves and a crystal grows, yet neither is alive. A tree never walks, yet it is alive. Check for cells first, then the rest of the list.

blocks.html: Life scientists answer questions with experiments. In math you met dependent and independent variables; an experiment uses the same idea. A test is fair when only one thing can explain the result.

Change one thing on purpose (the independent variable). Measure one thing (the dependent variable). Keep everything else the same (the controlled variables), and compare with a control group that gets the usual treatment or none. Repeat each group several times.

If two things change at once, either one could have caused the difference, and you cannot tell which. Holding the rest steady leaves only one possible cause. Repeating trials matters because living things vary: one plant may simply be a strong seedling.

blocks.name: bi-chart
blocks.cap: A fair test: only the fertilizer changed. The bars are means of five plants; the lines show how much the plants varied.

blocks.title: Name the variables
blocks.q: Leo asks, "Does fertilizer change how many tomatoes a plant makes?" He gives three groups 0 g, 5 g or 10 g each week.
steps: He changes the fertilizer: that is the independent variable.
He counts tomatoes: that is the dependent variable.
Water, sunlight, pot size and the kind of tomato stay the same: controlled variables.
The 0 g group is the control group.
blocks.a: Independent: fertilizer. Dependent: number of tomatoes.

blocks.title: Find the problem
blocks.q: Maya puts plant A in a dark closet and plant B in a sunny window. She also waters B twice as often. B grows taller. What can she conclude?
steps: Two things differ: light and water.
Either one could explain the taller plant.
blocks.a: Nothing certain. She must change only the light and water both plants the same.

blocks.title: Use the mean
blocks.q: Three tomato plants with 5 g of fertilizer make 12, 15 and 12 tomatoes. What is the mean?
steps: Divide by the number of plants: $39 \div 3 = 13$.

blocks.html: Changing two things at once (more light and more water), or leaving out the control group. Check: list everything that differs between groups. The list should hold exactly one item.

blocks.html: Most cells are far too small to see. A light microscope makes them look bigger with two lenses: the eyepiece you look into and an objective lens just above the slide. You will need multiplication to find how strong it is.

blocks.name: bi-microscope
blocks.cap: Tap a part to see its name.

blocks.html: Total magnification = eyepiece power × objective power. A 10× eyepiece with a 40× objective gives $10 \times 40 = 400$×. Higher power shows a smaller area of the slide, looking larger.

The objective makes an image 40 times wider than the cell. The eyepiece then magnifies that image 10 times more. Each lens multiplies what the one before it made, so the powers multiply, they do not add. The circle you look through stays the same size, so when everything looks 4 times wider, only a quarter as much of the slide fits across.

blocks.name: bi-microscope
blocks.cap: Switch objectives and watch the field of view shrink as the cells grow larger.

blocks.title: Total magnification
blocks.q: A microscope has a 10× eyepiece and a 100× objective. What is the total magnification?
steps: Multiply: $10 \times 100 = 1000$.

blocks.title: Working backward
blocks.q: You see a cell at 400× with a 10× eyepiece. Which objective are you using?
steps: Total = eyepiece × objective.
Objective = $400 \div 10 = 40$.

items: Start with the lowest-power objective and focus with the coarse knob.
Center what you want to see, then turn to a higher power.
At high power, focus only with the fine knob.
Use the diaphragm to adjust the light; high power often needs more.

blocks.html: Adding the powers: 10× and 40× is not 50×. Check with a story: if one lens makes it 4 times bigger and the next makes that 10 times bigger, it is now 40 times bigger, not 14. Another slip is expecting to see more of the slide at high power; you see less of it, larger.

blocks.html: Once you can use a microscope, you can measure with it. The bright circle you see is the field of view. If you know how wide it is, you can estimate the size of a cell by how many fit across. Cells are small, so we measure them in micrometers (µm), using powers of 10.
1 mm = 1,000 µm. The field of view shrinks as power grows: at 4 times the power it is a quarter as wide. Cell size ≈ field of view ÷ number of cells that fit across.

Field width × magnification stays the same. If a field 4.5 mm wide at 40× is viewed at 400× (10 times the power), everything looks 10 times wider, so only $4.5 \div 10 = 0.45$ mm of the slide fits in the circle.

blocks.name: bi-microscope
blocks.cap: Onion-like cells at 100×. Count about how many fit across the dashed line.

head: Total magnification
Field of view (mm)
Field of view (µm)
blocks.cap: One microscope with a field of 4.5 mm at 40×.

blocks.title: New power, new field
blocks.q: At 40× the field is 4.5 mm. How wide is it at 100×?
steps: The power grows $100 \div 40 = 2.5$ times.
The field shrinks 2.5 times: $4.5 \div 2.5 = 1.8$ mm.

blocks.title: Estimate a cell
blocks.q: At 100× (field 1.8 mm), about 6 cells fit end to end across the field. How long is one cell?
steps: Change to micrometers: $1.8 \times 1000 = 1800$ µm.
Share among 6 cells: $1800 \div 6 = 300$ µm.

blocks.title: Change units
blocks.q: A red blood cell is about 0.008 mm across. How many micrometers is that?
steps: Multiply by 1,000: $0.008 \times 1000 = 8$.

blocks.html: Forgetting that the field shrinks at higher power, or mixing millimeters and micrometers by a factor of 1,000. Check: a cell you need a microscope to see should come out between about 1 and a few hundred µm.

blocks.html: The first of the characteristics of life is that living things are made of cells. That idea took about two hundred years of looking through microscopes to settle, and today it is one of the foundations of biology: the cell theory.

The cell theory has three parts. (1) All living things are made of one or more cells. (2) The cell is the basic unit of structure and function in living things. (3) All cells come from cells that already existed.

head: Year
Scientist
What they found
rows: Looked at thin slices of cork and named the tiny boxes "cells".
Saw living single-celled organisms in pond water with his own lenses.
Concluded that plants are made of cells.
Concluded that animals are made of cells too.
Argued that every cell comes from another cell.
blocks.cap: How the cell theory was built.

blocks.name: bi-cell
blocks.cap: Switch between an animal cell, a plant cell and a bacterium. All three are cells.

blocks.html: Every living thing scientists have examined, from bacteria to whales, turns out to be made of cells. And no one has ever seen a cell form from nonliving matter: new cells appear only when an existing cell divides. The theory holds because every test so far agrees with it.

blocks.title: Which part?
blocks.q: A scientist watches one yeast cell split into two. Which part of the cell theory does this support?
steps: The observation is about where new cells come from.
The two new cells came from one cell that already existed.
blocks.a: All cells come from existing cells.

blocks.title: Is it made of cells?
blocks.q: Is a mushroom made of cells?
steps: A mushroom is a living thing (a fungus).
Every living thing is made of cells.

blocks.html: Thinking only animals, or only large living things, are made of cells, or that cells can form from mud or broth. Plants, fungi, protists and bacteria are all made of cells, and new cells come only from existing cells. Check: if it is alive, it is made of cells.

blocks.html: The cell theory says the cell is the basic unit of life. Some living things are just one cell. Others are built from trillions.

A unicellular organism is one cell that does every job of life: bacteria, amoebas, paramecia and yeast. A multicellular organism is made of many cells that specialize, each kind doing certain jobs: trees, mushrooms, insects and people.

blocks.name: bi-classify

cards.why: Yeast is a fungus that lives as single cells.
A mushroom is a fungus made of many threadlike cells.

blocks.cap: Sort the organisms: one cell or many?

blocks.html: A single cell must take in food, get rid of wastes, respond and divide all by itself, and it does. In a multicellular body, cells share the work. A red blood cell carries oxygen, a nerve cell carries signals and a muscle cell contracts. Each depends on the others for everything else.

blocks.name: bi-cell
blocks.cap: A bacterium: one whole living thing in one cell.

blocks.title: Bigger body, bigger cells?
blocks.q: An elephant is much bigger than a mouse. Are its cells bigger?
steps: Cells must stay small to move materials in and out quickly.
Most animal cells are a similar, tiny size.
The elephant is bigger because it has far more cells.
blocks.a: No. It has many more cells of about the same size.

blocks.title: Who does the job?
blocks.q: Which cell in a plant takes in water from the soil?
steps: Root hair cells grow long, thin extensions into the soil.
That shape gives a lot of surface to take in water.

blocks.html: Thinking a single-celled organism is too simple to be alive, or that big organisms have big cells. A paramecium does every job of life on its own. An elephant's cells are about the size of a mouse's; it simply has more.

blocks.html: Every cell, from a bacterium to one of your nerve cells, has a few parts in common. Learn these three first; the other organelles come next.

The cell membrane surrounds the cell and controls what goes in and out. The cytoplasm is the jelly-like inside where many reactions happen. In plants, animals, fungi and protists, the nucleus holds the DNA, the cell's instructions. Bacteria have no nucleus.

blocks.name: bi-cell
blocks.cap: The three main parts of an animal cell. Tap any part to see its job.

blocks.html: A cell needs food and water to get in and wastes to get out, but it must keep its own useful molecules inside. A membrane that let nothing through would starve the cell; one that let everything through would spill it. So the membrane is selectively permeable: some things pass, others do not.

blocks.name: bi-cell
blocks.cap: A bacterium has no nucleus. Tap to find where its DNA is.

blocks.title: Name the part
blocks.q: Which part of a cell holds its DNA?
steps: In plant, animal, fungus and protist cells, the DNA is kept inside the nucleus.

blocks.title: Every cell?
blocks.q: Does a bacterium have a nucleus? Does it have a membrane?
steps: Bacteria keep their DNA in a loop in the cytoplasm, with no nucleus around it.
Every cell has a membrane, bacteria included.
blocks.a: No nucleus, but yes, a membrane.

blocks.html: Thinking the membrane is a solid wall that blocks everything, or that the nucleus is the cell's "brain" doing every job. The membrane lets some things through. The nucleus stores the instructions; other parts, like ribosomes and mitochondria, do the work.

blocks.html: Inside the membrane and cytoplasm, cells of plants, animals, fungi and protists have small working parts called organelles. Many are wrapped in their own membranes.

head: Organelle
Job
Like a factory's …
rows: Release the energy stored in food, using oxygen
Folds and finishes proteins made by its ribosomes
Packages proteins and ships them out
Break down wastes and worn-out parts
blocks.cap: The main organelles and their jobs.

blocks.name: bi-cell
blocks.cap: Find the mitochondria. Then tap other parts to read their jobs.

blocks.html: Each organelle does a job, and they work as a team: ribosomes on the rough ER build a protein, the ER folds it, the Golgi packages it, and a small bubble carries it to the membrane.

Mitochondria do not create energy. Energy is never made from nothing; it only changes form. Sugar from food holds chemical energy. Mitochondria use oxygen to break the sugar down and pass its energy to a molecule called ATP that the rest of the cell can use.

blocks.title: Busy cells
blocks.q: Muscle cells in your legs work hard. Which organelle would you expect them to have a lot of?
steps: Hard work takes a lot of energy.
Mitochondria release energy from food.

blocks.title: Follow a protein
blocks.q: A cell makes a protein to send outside. Which organelles does it pass through, in order?
steps: Built by ribosomes on the rough ER.
Folded in the rough ER.
Packaged by the Golgi apparatus.
Carried in a bubble to the membrane, then released.

blocks.html: Saying mitochondria "make energy." They release energy stored in food. Check by tracing it back: the energy in sugar came from sunlight captured by a plant.

blocks.html: Plant and animal cells share the organelles you just met. Plant cells add three parts of their own.
Plant cells have a cell wall, chloroplasts and a large central vacuole; animal cells have none of these. Both have a membrane, cytoplasm, a nucleus, mitochondria, ribosomes, ER and a Golgi apparatus.

blocks.name: bi-cell
blocks.cap: Switch between the plant cell and the animal cell. What does the plant cell have that the animal cell lacks?

head: Part
Plant cell
Animal cell
rows: Large central vacuole (keeps the cell firm)
blocks.cap: Plant and animal cells compared.

blocks.html: Each extra part fits a plant's way of life. A plant cannot move to find food, so chloroplasts make it from light. It has no skeleton, so stiff walls and water-filled vacuoles hold it up; a wilting plant is one whose vacuoles have lost water. But a plant still has to use its sugar, so it needs mitochondria too.

blocks.title: Night shift
blocks.q: At night, which organelle releases energy from sugar in a leaf cell?
steps: There is no light, so the chloroplasts are not making sugar.
Mitochondria keep breaking down sugar made during the day.

blocks.title: Identify the cell
blocks.q: A cell under the microscope has a stiff outer wall and green oval bodies. Plant or animal?
steps: A wall and chloroplasts are found only in plant cells.

blocks.html: Thinking plant cells have chloroplasts instead of mitochondria. They have both: chloroplasts make sugar, and mitochondria release its energy, day and night. Check: a plant in the dark stays alive for days, living on stored sugar.

blocks.html: Why don't cells just grow bigger? The answer is geometry. You know how to find surface area and volume. A cell takes in food and gets rid of wastes through its surface, but its whole volume needs them.

blocks.name: lifesci-cubes
blocks.cap: Cubes of side 1, 2 and 4 µm. Move the slider to grow the last cube.

blocks.html: When a cell gets wider, its volume grows faster than its surface. Double the width: the surface area grows 4 times, but the volume grows 8 times. So a large cell has too little surface for its inside, and small cells exchange materials faster.

Surface area uses side × side, so it grows with the square of the width. Volume uses side × side × side, so it grows with the cube. For a cube, surface area ÷ volume $= 6s^2 \div s^3 = 6 \div s$: the bigger $s$ gets, the smaller this ratio.

blocks.title: Find the ratio
blocks.q: A cube-shaped cell has sides of 2 µm. Find its surface area, its volume and the ratio.
steps: Surface area: $6 \times 2 \times 2 = 24$ µm².
Volume: $2 \times 2 \times 2 = 8$ µm³.
Ratio: $24 \div 8 = 3$.

blocks.title: Doubling the width
blocks.q: The cell grows to 4 µm on each side. How do its surface and volume change?
steps: Surface area: $6 \times 4 \times 4 = 96$ µm², which is $96 \div 24 = 4$ times as much.
Volume: $4 \times 4 \times 4 = 64$ µm³, which is $64 \div 8 = 8$ times as much.
Ratio: $96 \div 64 = 1.5$, half of what it was.
blocks.a: Surface ×4, volume ×8, ratio cut in half.

blocks.name: bi-chart
blocks.cap: The ratio falls fast as a cell grows.

blocks.html: Thinking a cell that doubles in width doubles its surface and volume too. Surface grows 4 times and volume 8 times. Check with small cubes: a 2 × 2 × 2 cube is built from 8 unit cubes.

blocks.html: The cell membrane lets some materials through. Many of them cross without the cell spending any energy, simply because particles are always moving.

Diffusion: particles spread from where they are more crowded to where they are less crowded. Osmosis: the diffusion of water across a membrane, toward the side with more dissolved material (less water).

blocks.name: bi-membrane
blocks.cap: Particles diffusing across a membrane. Watch until the two sides even out.

blocks.html: Particles move at random. Where they are crowded, more of them happen to wander away than wander in, so they spread out. Once they are even, they keep moving, but as many cross each way as the other: a balance called equilibrium. Water does the same. A salty side has fewer free water molecules, so more water crosses into it than out of it.

blocks.name: bi-membrane
blocks.cap: Try each solution with a plant cell and a red blood cell.

blocks.title: Oxygen in the lungs
blocks.q: The air sacs in your lungs have more oxygen than the blood flowing past them. Which way does oxygen move?
steps: Particles diffuse from more crowded to less crowded.
blocks.a: From the air sacs into the blood.

blocks.title: A cell in salt water
blocks.q: A cell with 1% salt inside sits in 5% salt water. The membrane lets water through but not salt. What happens?
steps: Water moves toward the side with more dissolved salt.
The outside is saltier.
Water leaves the cell, and it shrinks.
blocks.a: Water moves out; the cell shrinks.

blocks.title: Limp celery
blocks.q: Why does limp celery get crisp in plain water?
steps: The celery cells have more dissolved material than plain water.
Water moves into the cells, which swell and press against their walls.
blocks.a: Water enters the cells by osmosis.

blocks.html: Thinking water moves toward the side with more water, or that particles stop once they are spread evenly. Water moves toward the saltier side. At equilibrium the particles keep moving, in both directions at the same rate.

blocks.html: In a multicellular organism, cells specialize. Cells of the same kind work together, and those groups work together too. Biologists name the levels from small to large.
Cell → tissue (similar cells doing one job) → organ (several tissues working together) → organ system (organs working together) → organism.

head: Level
Animal example
Plant example
blocks.cap: The five levels, with examples.

blocks.name: bi-body
blocks.cap: The digestive system: organs working together. Tap an organ.

blocks.html: No single kind of cell could do an organ's whole job. The stomach must churn food, make digestive juices and respond to signals, so it has muscle tissue, lining tissue and nerve tissue all working at once. Organs then team up: the stomach can only do its part because the mouth, intestines and liver do theirs.

blocks.title: Name the level
blocks.q: Which level is the heart?
steps: The heart has muscle tissue, nerve tissue and lining tissue working together.
Several tissues together make an organ.

blocks.title: Put in order
blocks.q: Order these from smallest to largest: nervous system, nerve cell, brain, nerve tissue.
steps: Start with one cell: nerve cell.
Many nerve cells make nerve tissue.
The brain is an organ built of nerve tissue and more.
The brain, spinal cord and nerves form the nervous system.
blocks.a: Nerve cell → nerve tissue → brain → nervous system.

blocks.html: Placing organs below tissues, or thinking an organ is made of one kind of cell. An organ is built from several tissues. Check: can it do a big job on its own, like pumping or digesting? Then it is at least an organ.

blocks.html: Scientists have named well over a million kinds of living things. To keep track, they sort them into groups inside groups, by the traits they share, much like a library sorts books into sections, shelves and rows. Every group is built on the characteristics of life and on traits of the body and cells.

The eight main ranks, from broadest to narrowest: domain, kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species. Each rank holds fewer kinds of organisms that share more traits. A memory trick: Dear King Philip Came Over For Good Soup.

head: Rank
Gray wolf
House cat
blocks.cap: A wolf and a cat share every rank down to order.

blocks.html: The kingdom Animalia holds every animal: sponges, insects, fish and you. The order Carnivora holds only meat-eating mammals like wolves, cats and bears. The genus Canis holds just wolves, coyotes and their close kin. As you go down, each group gets smaller and its members get more alike.

blocks.name: bi-tree
blocks.cap: A family tree of vertebrates. Animals that share more branches share more ranks.

blocks.title: Which holds more?
blocks.q: Which holds more kinds of organisms: a class or a genus?
steps: Class comes higher in the list than genus.
Higher ranks are broader and hold more kinds.

blocks.title: Closest shared rank
blocks.q: The lion is Panthera leo and the tiger is Panthera tigris. What is the narrowest rank they share?
steps: Both are in the genus Panthera.
Their species differ.

blocks.html: Thinking a "higher" rank like kingdom holds fewer organisms because it sounds more important. The broadest ranks hold the most kinds; the species holds just one. Check: is every cat an animal? Yes, so the animal kingdom must be bigger than the cat family.

blocks.html: One animal can have many common names: cougar, mountain lion, puma, panther. Scientists everywhere use one name instead. The system comes from the ranks: each species gets a two-part name, its genus and then a specific name.

A scientific name is genus + specific name, like Canis lupus for the gray wolf. The genus starts with a capital letter, the specific name is all lowercase, and the whole name is printed in italics (underlined when handwritten).

Carl Linnaeus made this two-part system standard, for plants in 1753 and for animals in 1758. Because the first word is the genus, the name itself tells you something: animals that share a genus are close relatives. Canis lupus (gray wolf) and Canis latrans (coyote) are close kin; Vulpes vulpes (red fox) is in another genus.

blocks.name: bi-classify

cards.why: Same second word as the black bear, but a different genus: a lobster is not a bear.
"Rubrum" just means red. The genus Acer is the maples.

blocks.cap: Sort by genus. Watch out for shared second words.

blocks.title: Write it right
blocks.q: How do you write the scientific name of the human?
steps: Genus: Homo, with a capital H.
Specific name: sapiens, all lowercase.
Print it in italics.

blocks.title: Close relatives?
blocks.q: Which two are most closely related: Ursus americanus, Homarus americanus, Ursus arctos?
steps: Compare the first words: two are Ursus.
The shared word "americanus" only means "from America".

blocks.html: Capitalizing both words, or thinking two species with the same second word are relatives. Only the genus is capitalized, and only a shared genus shows close kinship. Check the first word, not the second.

blocks.html: Field guides help you name an organism you do not know. Many use a dichotomous key: "dichotomous" means "cut in two." It turns classifying into a path of either-or choices.

A dichotomous key is a list of numbered steps. Each step gives two choices about a trait you can observe. Pick the one that fits, and it sends you to another step or gives the organism's name. Always start at step 1.

blocks.name: bi-key

steps.a: Its wings are covered with colored scales
steps.b: Its wings are clear and its body is fuzzy and striped

blocks.cap: Tap a specimen, then walk it through the key.

blocks.html: Each choice splits the remaining possibilities into two groups, so every step rules out a share of them. The traits are things anyone can check, like legs or wings, so two people using the same key on the same specimen reach the same name.

blocks.title: Walk the key
blocks.q: A specimen has six legs and wings covered with colored scales. Use the key above.
steps: Step 1: it has legs, so go to step 2.
Step 2: six legs, so go to step 3.
Step 3: it has wings, so go to step 5.
Step 5: colored scales on its wings.

blocks.title: No legs
blocks.q: A specimen has no legs and a shell. What is it?
steps: Step 1: no legs, so go to step 4.
Step 4: it has a shell.

blocks.html: Jumping ahead or answering from what you think the organism is ("It looks like a bee, so it is a bee"). Read both choices at every step, in order, and go only where the key sends you. Check by writing down the steps you used: 1 → 2 → 3 → 5.

blocks.html: The broadest rank is the domain. It sorts life by the kind of cells it has. You learned in Membrane, Cytoplasm and Nucleus that some cells have no nucleus; that difference splits life at the top.
Life has three domains. Bacteria and Archaea are single cells with no nucleus. Eukarya have cells with a nucleus, and include four kingdoms: protists, fungi, plants and animals.

blocks.html: In the 1970s Carl Woese compared the RNA in cells and found that some single cells without a nucleus were as different from bacteria as bacteria are from us. He and his colleagues proposed the three domains in 1990. Comparing DNA also shows that fungi are more closely related to animals than to plants.

blocks.cap: Tap fungi and animals, then fungi and plants: which pair shares a more recent ancestor?

blocks.title: Place a mushroom
blocks.q: A mushroom grows in one place. Which kingdom is it in?
steps: It has no chlorophyll and cannot make food.
It absorbs food from what it grows on, and its walls are made of chitin.

blocks.title: Place a single cell
blocks.q: One cell with a nucleus swims in pond water. Which domain?
steps: A nucleus means Eukarya, even for one cell.

blocks.html: Putting fungi with plants because both stay in one place, or bacteria with animals because some move. Sort by cells and food: fungi absorb food and have chitin walls. Check: can it make its own food? If not, it is not a plant.

blocks.html: Bacteria are the domain you met in Three Domains and the Kingdoms: single cells with no nucleus. They are tiny (a typical one is 1 to 2 µm long) and they live almost everywhere: in soil, water, hot springs, ice, and on and inside you.
A bacterium is one cell with a cell wall, a membrane, cytoplasm, ribosomes and a loop of DNA, but no nucleus. Most bacteria are harmless or helpful; only a small share cause disease.

blocks.name: bi-cell
blocks.cap: A bacterium. Tap each part to read its job.

blocks.html: Life on Earth depends on bacteria. They break down dead plants and animals so the nutrients return to the soil. Some live in bumps on the roots of beans and peas and turn nitrogen from the air into a form plants can use. Others turn milk into yogurt, and the ones in your gut help break down food. Most strains of E. coli, for example, live harmlessly in the intestines of people and animals.

blocks.title: What is missing?
blocks.q: Which of these does a bacterium lack: a membrane, ribosomes, a nucleus, DNA?
steps: A bacterium has a membrane, ribosomes and DNA, like every cell.
Its DNA lies loose in the cytoplasm.

blocks.title: Helpful or not?
blocks.q: A farmer plants beans in a field to add nitrogen to the soil. Who does the work?
steps: Bacteria living in the bean roots turn nitrogen gas from the air into a form plants use.

blocks.html: Thinking all bacteria are germs that make people sick. Only a small share cause disease; many are needed, from the bacteria that recycle dead leaves to the ones that help digest food. Check: name one food made with bacteria (yogurt, cheese, sauerkraut).

blocks.html: A bacterium multiplies by splitting in two. It copies its DNA, grows, and divides into two new cells. Then each of those divides. This is a place to use exponents.

With food and warmth, the number of bacteria doubles each generation: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 … After $n$ generations, one bacterium becomes $2^n$; a starting number $N$ becomes $N \times 2^n$. Growth slows and stops when food and space run out.

blocks.name: bi-population
blocks.cap: Six generations of doubling, from one bacterium.

blocks.html: Every bacterium divides, the new ones included, so the number is multiplied by 2 each time, not increased by 2. That is why the counts take off. In ideal lab conditions E. coli can divide about every 20 minutes, so one cell could become $2^{3} = 8$ in an hour and $2^{30}$, over a billion, in ten hours, if nothing ran out.

blocks.title: Count the doublings
blocks.q: One bacterium divides every generation. How many are there after 5 generations?

blocks.title: Use the time
blocks.q: A sample starts with 10 bacteria that divide every 30 minutes. How many after 2 hours?
steps: Generations: $120 \div 30 = 4$.
Number: $10 \times 2^4 = 10 \times 16 = 160$.

blocks.name: bi-population
blocks.cap: Doubling forever (J-curve) compared with real growth that levels off when food and space run out (S-curve).

blocks.html: Adding 2 each generation (2, 4, 6, 8) instead of doubling (2, 4, 8, 16), or expecting doubling to go on forever. Check: each generation should be twice the one before. And in any real dish, food runs low and wastes build up, so the curve levels off.

blocks.html: Viruses cause colds and flu, so people often lump them in with bacteria. They are very different. A virus is not even a cell.

A virus is genetic material (DNA or RNA) inside a protein coat. It has no membrane, cytoplasm or ribosomes of its own, so it can make copies of itself only inside a living host cell. Most viruses are about 20 to 300 nanometers across, far smaller than bacteria.

blocks.name: lifesci-scale
blocks.cap: Sizes to scale. Switch between a cell with bacteria and a bacterium with viruses.

blocks.html: A virus attaches to a host cell and gets its genetic material inside. The cell's own ribosomes and supplies then build new virus parts, which assemble into new viruses and leave the cell. Outside a cell, a virus does nothing at all: it does not eat, grow or use energy. That is why scientists still debate whether viruses count as alive.

blocks.title: How small?
blocks.q: A bacterium is 2 µm long. A virus is 100 nm across. About how many such viruses fit along the bacterium? (1 µm = 1,000 nm)
steps: Bacterium: $2 \times 1000 = 2000$ nm.
Viruses in a row: $2000 \div 100 = 20$.

blocks.title: Antibiotics?
blocks.q: Will an antibiotic act on a cold virus?
steps: Antibiotics damage parts of bacterial cells, such as the cell wall or ribosomes.
A virus has no cell wall and no ribosomes of its own.
blocks.a: No. Antibiotics do not work on viruses.

blocks.html: Thinking viruses are tiny bacteria and that antibiotics work on them. Viruses are far smaller, are not cells, and antibiotics do not act on them (CDC). Check: does it have its own ribosomes? Bacteria do; viruses do not.
Vaccines work by training the immune system to remember a virus, so it can respond quickly later. How the body defends itself comes in the Human Body unit.

OpenStax, Biology 2e, 21.2 Virus Infections and Hosts

CDC, Antibiotic Do's and Don'ts

blocks.html: Look at a drop of pond water under a microscope and you will likely see protists: mostly single cells, but each with a nucleus. They are in the domain Eukarya, with the fungi, plants and animals, but they belong to none of those kingdoms.

Protists are eukaryotes that are not plants, animals or fungi. They are often grouped by how they get food: animal-like (amoebas, paramecia hunt and move), plant-like (algae, diatoms make food by photosynthesis) and fungus-like (water molds and slime molds absorb food).

blocks.name: bi-classify

cards.text: Amoeba: engulfs food with false feet
Diatom: photosynthesis in a glassy shell

cards.why: Kelp is a many-celled alga: a protist that makes food by photosynthesis.

cards.text: Slime mold: feeds on rotting wood

blocks.cap: Sort the protists by how they get food.

blocks.html: Protists are a "leftover" group: everything with a nucleus that is not a plant, animal or fungus. That is why they vary so much. Some are as big as a forest (kelp), most are single cells, and many are much larger than bacteria, so you can often see them at 100×.

blocks.name: bi-microscope
blocks.cap: At 100×, a pond-water protist can stretch across a good part of the view.

blocks.title: Bacterium or protist?
blocks.q: A single cell from pond water has a nucleus. Is it a bacterium?
steps: Bacteria never have a nucleus.
blocks.a: No. It is most likely a protist.

blocks.title: How does it move?
blocks.q: How do an amoeba, a paramecium and a euglena move?
steps: Amoeba: pseudopods ("false feet") that flow forward.
Paramecium: thousands of tiny hairs called cilia.
Euglena: one whip-like flagellum.

blocks.html: Thinking every microscopic organism is a bacterium. Protists have a nucleus and are often much larger. Check: does it have a nucleus? Then it is not a bacterium.

OpenStax, Biology 2e, 23.3 Diversity of Protists

blocks.html: Fungi are the kingdom that is easiest to mistake for plants. In Three Domains and the Kingdoms you saw why they are not: they cannot make food, and they are more closely related to animals.
Fungi include yeasts (single cells), molds and mushrooms. They absorb food from what they grow on. Their cell walls contain chitin. Many are decomposers, breaking down dead matter.

A fungus releases digestive juices into wood, soil or bread, then absorbs the small molecules that result. Most of a fungus is a hidden web of thin threads called hyphae. A mushroom is only the part that pops up to release spores, a bit like an apple on an apple tree.

blocks.name: bi-foodweb
blocks.cap: A forest food web. The mushroom and earthworm are decomposers.

head: Fungus
What it does
rows: Breaks down sugar and gives off carbon dioxide gas, which makes bread rise
Makes penicillin, the antibiotic Alexander Fleming discovered in 1928
Break down fallen logs and leaves, returning nutrients to the soil
Grows on and spoils old bread
blocks.cap: Some fungi and their jobs.

blocks.title: Plant or not?
blocks.q: Is a mushroom a plant?
steps: Plants make food by photosynthesis; a mushroom has no chlorophyll.
It absorbs food, and its walls contain chitin.

blocks.title: Bread
blocks.q: Why does bread dough with yeast rise?
steps: Yeast cells break down sugar in the dough.
They give off carbon dioxide gas, which forms bubbles.
blocks.a: Gas from the yeast puffs it up.

blocks.html: Thinking mushrooms are plants. Fungi have no chlorophyll and cannot make food, and the mushroom is only a small part of a fungus whose threads spread through soil or wood. Check: does it need light to grow? Fungi do not.

blocks.html: You have now met bacteria, viruses, protists and fungi. Together they are called microbes. People mostly hear about the harmful ones, but those are a small share.

Microbes make foods like yogurt, cheese and bread, recycle nutrients, and live in our bodies. A few cause disease. Different microbes are different kinds of life, so the medicine that acts on one may do nothing to another: antibiotics act on bacteria, not viruses.

blocks.name: bi-classify
blocks.cap: Helpful or harmful?

head: Illness
Caused by

blocks.html: Antibiotics work by damaging parts that bacterial cells have, such as their walls or ribosomes. Viruses have none of these parts, so antibiotics cannot touch them. Washing hands with soap and water removes many germs of all kinds, because soap lifts microbes off the skin so water can rinse them away (CDC).

blocks.title: Match the medicine
blocks.q: Could an antibiotic act on what causes strep throat? On what causes a cold?
steps: Strep throat is caused by a bacterium: yes.
A cold is caused by a virus: no.
blocks.a: Strep throat yes; a cold no.

blocks.title: Sort it
blocks.q: Is the mold that makes penicillin helpful or harmful?
steps: Penicillin is a medicine that acts on many bacteria.

blocks.html: Thinking every microbe is harmful and that one medicine works on all of them. Most microbes are harmless or helpful, and antibiotics do nothing against a virus. Check: first ask what kind of microbe it is.

blocks.html: In Plant Cells and Animal Cells you saw that plant cells have chloroplasts. Here is what they do. (Young learners met the idea in Plants Make Their Own Food.)

In chloroplasts, plants use light energy to turn carbon dioxide and water into sugar (glucose), giving off oxygen: 6CO₂ + 6H₂O + light → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂. The sugar stores the energy and is the raw material for the plant's whole body.

blocks.name: bi-energy
blocks.cap: Inputs and outputs of a chloroplast.

blocks.html: Where does a tree's mass come from? In the 1600s Jan Baptist van Helmont grew a 5-pound willow in 200 pounds of dried soil, giving it only water. Five years later the tree weighed about 169 pounds, and the soil had lost only about 2 ounces. Today we know most of the missing mass came from the air: the carbon in wood, leaves and roots comes from carbon dioxide, joined with water.

blocks.name: bi-plant
blocks.cap: Carbon dioxide enters the leaf, water rises from the roots, oxygen leaves.

blocks.title: Inputs and outputs
blocks.q: Which are the inputs of photosynthesis, and which the outputs?
steps: Inputs: carbon dioxide, water, and light energy.
Outputs: sugar (glucose) and oxygen.
blocks.a: In: CO₂, water, light. Out: sugar, oxygen.

blocks.title: Count molecules
blocks.q: How many molecules of carbon dioxide does a leaf use to make 3 molecules of glucose?
steps: The equation uses 6 CO₂ for each glucose.

blocks.title: Where the mass comes from
blocks.q: A tree gains 50 kg while its soil loses 40 g. Did its mass come from the soil?
steps: 40 g is $0.04$ kg, less than 0.1% of 50 kg.
The rest came from carbon dioxide and water.
blocks.a: No, almost all of it came from air and water.

blocks.html: Thinking plants get their food and mass from the soil. Soil gives water and small amounts of minerals. Almost all of a plant's mass comes from carbon dioxide in the air and from water. Light brings energy, not mass.

blocks.html: Photosynthesis stores energy in sugar. Every cell needs to get that energy back out. The process that does it is cellular respiration, and it happens mostly in the mitochondria.

Cells release the energy in sugar by combining it with oxygen: C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O + energy. The energy is stored in a molecule called ATP, which powers the cell's work. Every living cell does it, plant cells included, day and night.

blocks.name: bi-energy
blocks.cap: Inputs and outputs of a mitochondrion.

blocks.html: A cell needs energy every moment: to build proteins, move materials, divide and keep itself in order. Sugar holds energy in its chemical bonds. Breaking sugar down step by step, with oxygen, releases that energy in small amounts the cell can catch as ATP. A plant's cells must do this even in sunlight, because chloroplasts make sugar but do not power the rest of the cell.

blocks.title: Breathing or respiration?
blocks.q: How is breathing related to cellular respiration?
steps: Breathing moves air in and out of the lungs.
Cellular respiration is the chemical process in every cell.
Breathing brings in the oxygen that respiration uses and removes the carbon dioxide it makes.
blocks.a: They are different, but breathing supplies respiration.

blocks.title: Count molecules
blocks.q: A cell breaks down 4 molecules of glucose. How many molecules of oxygen does it use?
steps: Each glucose uses 6 O₂.

blocks.title: Plants in the dark
blocks.q: A bean plant sits in a sealed jar in a dark closet. What happens to the carbon dioxide?
steps: In the dark there is no photosynthesis.
The plant's cells keep respiring and give off carbon dioxide.

blocks.html: Thinking respiration means breathing, or that plants photosynthesize instead of respiring. Respiration is the chemical process in every cell, and plant cells do it too. Check: a plant in the dark stays alive, so its cells must still be releasing energy.

OpenStax, Concepts of Biology, 4.3 Citric Acid Cycle and Oxidative Phosphorylation

blocks.html: Put photosynthesis and cellular respiration side by side, and a pattern appears: each one uses what the other makes.

The outputs of photosynthesis (sugar and oxygen) are the inputs of respiration, and the outputs of respiration (carbon dioxide and water) are the inputs of photosynthesis. Matter cycles; energy flows in as light and is used up as the cell works.

blocks.name: bi-energy
blocks.cap: The cycle between chloroplasts and mitochondria.

head: Photosynthesis
Cellular respiration
blocks.cap: The two processes compared.

blocks.html: The atoms are reused, but the energy is not. Light energy is stored in sugar, then released by respiration to do work, and finally lost as heat. That is why life needs a steady supply of sunlight while the same carbon and oxygen atoms go around and around.

blocks.title: Plant under a lamp
blocks.q: A water plant sits in a sealed tube under a bright lamp. What happens to the carbon dioxide in the water?
steps: In bright light the plant photosynthesizes faster than it respires.
So it uses more carbon dioxide than it gives off.

blocks.title: Snail alone
blocks.q: A pond snail sits in a sealed tube under the same lamp, with no plant. What happens?
steps: The snail only respires; light does not change that.

blocks.html: Thinking the two are exact opposites happening in the same place. They form a cycle of matter, but photosynthesis happens in chloroplasts and respiration in mitochondria, and only photosynthesis needs light. Check: at night, which one still happens? Respiration.

blocks.html: A leaf needs water for photosynthesis, but the water is in the soil, sometimes 100 meters below the top of a tall tree. And the roots need sugar, which is made in the leaves. Plants solve both problems with two kinds of tubes.

Xylem carries water and minerals up from the roots. Phloem carries sugar from the leaves to wherever it is used or stored, up or down. Water leaves the plant as vapor through tiny pores in the leaves called stomata.

blocks.name: bi-plant
blocks.cap: Water rises in the xylem; sugar moves in the phloem.

blocks.html: Most of the lift comes from the top, not the bottom. As water evaporates from the leaves (transpiration), it pulls on the water behind it. Water molecules cling to each other, so the whole thin column in the xylem is drawn upward, like drinking through a very long straw. Root pressure gives only a small push.

blocks.name: bi-plant
blocks.cap: Guard cells open the stomata when water is plentiful and close them when it is scarce.

blocks.title: Celery and food coloring
blocks.q: A celery stalk stands in blue water. After a day, blue dots show in the cut stalk. Which tubes are they?
steps: The blue water moved up the stalk.
Water moves up in the xylem.

blocks.title: Sugar to a potato
blocks.q: A potato grows underground. How does sugar from the leaves get there?
steps: Sugar is made in the leaves.
Phloem carries sugar down to the potato, where it is stored as starch.

blocks.html: Thinking water is pumped up from the roots like a heart pumps blood, or that xylem and phloem carry the same things. Most of the pull comes from water evaporating from the leaves. Check: when stomata close on a dry day, water flow slows.

OpenStax, Concepts of Biology, 14.1 The Plant Kingdom

blocks.html: One of the characteristics of life is responding to the surroundings. Plants cannot walk away from shade, but they respond by growing in a direction.
Plants grow toward light (phototropism), roots grow down with gravity while stems grow up (gravitropism), and vines and tendrils curl around what they touch (thigmotropism).

blocks.name: bi-plant
blocks.cap: Light from the left: the stem bends toward it.

blocks.html: A plant hormone called auxin collects on the shaded side of a stem. It makes the cells there grow longer than the cells on the lit side, so the stem bends toward the light. That puts the leaves where they can catch more light for photosynthesis. Roots growing down find water; tendrils that wrap around a support hold a vine up toward the sun.

blocks.name: bi-plant
blocks.cap: A seedling on its side: roots turn down and the stem turns up.

blocks.title: Name the response
blocks.q: A pea plant's tendril wraps around a fence wire. Which response is this?
steps: The tendril responds to touch.
"Thigmo" means touch.

blocks.title: A pot on its side
blocks.q: A potted bean seedling is laid on its side. What happens over a few days?
steps: Roots grow with gravity: they curve down.
The stem grows against gravity: it curves up.
blocks.a: Roots turn down, stem turns up.

blocks.html: Thinking plants cannot respond because they do not move from place to place. They respond by growing, and some move fast: a sensitive plant folds its leaves within seconds of a touch, and a Venus flytrap snaps shut. Try a window plant at home: turn the pot and watch it lean back toward the light over a few days (more ideas in Nature Study).

blocks.html: All plants make food by photosynthesis, but they differ in how they move water and how they spread. Those two traits sort the plant kingdom into four big groups.

head: Group
Tubes (xylem, phloem)?
Seeds?
Spreads by
Examples
blocks.cap: The four big plant groups.

blocks.html: Mosses have no tubes for water and stay small; ferns have tubes but no seeds; conifers make seeds in cones; flowering plants make seeds inside fruits.

blocks.name: bi-tree
blocks.cap: Each new trait on the tree is shared by every group above it.

blocks.html: Without xylem, water can only soak from cell to cell, a short trip, so mosses stay low and live in damp places. Tubes let ferns grow tall. Seeds carry a young plant with a food supply and a tough coat, so conifers and flowering plants can spread into dry places. Flowers and fruits add helpers: animals that carry pollen and seeds.

blocks.title: Which group?
blocks.q: A plant has tubes, makes no seeds, and has brown dots under its leaves. Which group?
steps: Tubes but no seeds: a fern.
The brown dots release spores.

blocks.title: Shared traits
blocks.q: Which traits do ferns and pine trees share?
steps: Both have tubes for water and live on land.
Only pines have seeds; neither has flowers.

blocks.html: Thinking every plant has flowers and seeds. Mosses and ferns spread by spores, and pine trees make seeds in cones without any flowers. Check the table: only one group has flowers.

blocks.html: Flowering plants make seeds inside fruits. The flower is where it starts. (Young learners met this in Flowers, Fruits and Seeds.)

blocks.name: bi-plant
blocks.cap: The parts of a flower, with a visiting bee.

blocks.html: The stamens make pollen. Pollination carries pollen to the pistil, often from another flower, by animals or wind. Then seeds form at the base of the pistil, and that part grows into the fruit around them.

items: Petals: color and scent that draw in pollinators.
Sepals: small leaf-like parts that protected the bud.
Pistil: catches pollen at its tip; seeds form at its base.

blocks.html: Flowers that need animals spend energy on bright petals, scent and nectar, the "pay" for the visit; the animal picks up pollen on one flower and leaves it on the next. Wind-pollinated flowers, like grasses, skip all that: they are small and plain and make huge amounts of light pollen.

blocks.title: Is it a fruit?
blocks.q: In botany, is a cucumber a fruit?
steps: A cucumber grows from the base of a flower's pistil.
It holds seeds.

blocks.title: Is it a fruit?
blocks.q: Is a carrot a fruit?
steps: A carrot is a root.
It does not grow from a flower or hold seeds.

blocks.html: Thinking a fruit is anything sweet and a vegetable anything not sweet. In botany, any part that develops from a flower and holds seeds is a fruit: tomatoes, peppers, pumpkins and bean pods too. "Vegetable" is a kitchen word, not a botany word.

blocks.name: bi-picture
blocks.cap: Fruits in the botanical sense, and other plant parts we eat.

blocks.html: Plant the same seeds in two gardens and they may grow very differently. A fair test can find out why.
A plant's growth depends on its genes and its surroundings: light, water, nutrients, temperature and space. Genes set what is possible; conditions decide how much of it happens.

blocks.name: bi-chart
blocks.cap: Same seeds, same water and soil, different light.

blocks.html: Seeds from one parent plant share most of their genes. If they grow differently, the difference must come from their surroundings. Two different varieties given the same care show the opposite: a dwarf pea stays short beside a tall pea, because their genes differ. Most traits depend on both.

blocks.title: Read the chart
blocks.q: How much taller, on average, were the plants with 12 hours of light than those with 2 hours?
steps: 12 hours: 23 cm. 2 hours: 6 cm.

blocks.title: Genes or surroundings?
blocks.q: A tall variety of corn grows short in poor, dry soil. Why?
steps: Its genes allow tall growth.
Poor soil and too little water limited it.
blocks.a: Both: the genes allow tall growth, but the conditions held it back.

blocks.html: Thinking a plant's size is decided by genes alone, or by care alone. Genes set the range; light, water, nutrients, temperature and space decide where in that range the plant ends up. Check: did the plants share genes, or share conditions?

blocks.html: The animal kingdom, from Three Domains and the Kingdoms, holds a huge range of creatures. The first big split is simple: does the animal have a backbone?

Vertebrates have a backbone (a spine made of small bones called vertebrae): fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals. Invertebrates have none: insects, spiders, worms, snails, jellyfish and many more. About 95 of every 100 named animal species are invertebrates.

blocks.name: bi-classify

cards.why: A jellyfish has no bones at all.

blocks.cap: Sort the animals: backbone or not?

blocks.html: A backbone protects the spinal cord and gives muscles a strong frame to pull on, which lets vertebrates grow large. But being large is not the same as being common. Insects alone count about a million named species, far more than all the vertebrates together. The animals we know best (pets, farm animals, zoo animals) are mostly vertebrates, which makes them seem typical.

blocks.title: Backbone or not?
blocks.q: Does an octopus have a backbone?
steps: An octopus is a mollusk, like a snail.
Mollusks have soft bodies and no bones.

blocks.title: Most animals
blocks.q: Out of 1,000 named animal species, about how many are invertebrates?
steps: About 95% are invertebrates.

blocks.html: Thinking most animals have backbones because the ones we know best do. Insects alone far outnumber all vertebrate species. Check: next time you are outside, count the kinds of animals you see. Most will be insects, spiders and other invertebrates.

blocks.html: Invertebrates are most of the animal kingdom. Biologists sort them into groups by their body plans.

head: Group
Body plan
Examples
rows: A body full of pores that filters food from water; stays in one place
Soft, jelly-like body with stinging tentacles
Long, soft body; earthworms have ring-shaped segments
Soft body, often a shell, a muscular foot
Jointed legs and a hard outer skeleton (exoskeleton)
Spiny skin, body in five parts around a center
blocks.cap: The major invertebrate groups.

blocks.html: Arthropods are the biggest group. They include insects (6 legs, 3 body parts), arachnids (8 legs, 2 body parts: spiders, scorpions, ticks) and crustaceans (crabs, lobsters, shrimp).

blocks.name: bi-picture
blocks.cap: One or more animals from most of the groups.

blocks.html: These groups are based on deep features of the body: how it is built, whether it has segments, what supports it. Where an animal lives does not decide its group. A jellyfish and a sea star live in the sea, but they have no backbone, gills or fins, so they are not fish.

blocks.title: Name the group
blocks.q: An animal has jointed legs, a hard exoskeleton, eight legs and two body parts. Which group?
steps: Jointed legs and an exoskeleton: an arthropod.
Eight legs and two body parts: an arachnid.

blocks.title: Spider or insect?
blocks.q: Is a spider an insect?
steps: Count legs: a spider has 8.
Insects have 6.
blocks.a: No. A spider is an arachnid.

blocks.html: Calling jellyfish and starfish fish, and spiders insects. Jellyfish are cnidarians, sea stars are echinoderms, and spiders are arachnids, a different arthropod group from insects. Check: count the legs and look for a backbone, gills and fins.

blocks.html: Vertebrates come in five familiar groups. Young learners met them one at a time, starting with Mammals. Here we compare them by their body traits.

head: Group
Covering
Breathes with

Examples
rows: Gills when young, then lungs and skin
blocks.cap: The five vertebrate groups.

blocks.html: Body traits decide the group, not where an animal lives or how it moves: hair and milk for mammals, feathers for birds, gills and fins for fish, dry scales and lungs for reptiles, moist skin for amphibians.

blocks.name: bi-classify

cards.why: A whale breathes air, has a little hair and feeds its young milk.
A bat has fur and feeds its young milk; its wings are skin, not feathers.
A penguin has feathers and a beak, even though it cannot fly.
A turtle has dry scales and lungs, even when it lives in water.
Moist skin, not scales: an amphibian.

blocks.cap: The tricky ones: sort by body traits.

blocks.html: Traits like hair, milk and feathers are shared by every member of a group because they were inherited from a common ancestor. Swimming or flying is not: whales swim like fish and bats fly like birds, but their bodies show who their relatives are.

blocks.title: A bat
blocks.q: Is a bat a bird?
steps: A bat has fur, not feathers.
It feeds its young milk.
blocks.a: No. A bat is a mammal.

blocks.title: A whale
blocks.q: Is a whale a fish?
steps: A whale breathes air with lungs and has no gills.
It has a little hair and feeds its young milk.
blocks.a: No. A whale is a mammal.

blocks.html: Sorting by habitat (whales as fish) or by flight (bats as birds). Check the body: hair and milk mean mammal; feathers mean bird; gills and fins mean fish.

blocks.html: Every vertebrate and invertebrate has a body suited to its way of life. A duck can paddle, a hawk can grip, a polar bear stays warm. These suited traits are called adaptations.

An adaptation is an inherited trait that helps an organism survive where it lives, such as a duck's webbed feet, a hawk's hooked beak and talons, or camouflage. Adaptations become common over many generations.

blocks.name: bi-habitat
blocks.cap: A pond. How is each animal's body suited to life here?

head: Organism
Adaptation
How it helps
blocks.cap: Body adaptations and what they do.

blocks.html: In any population, individuals differ a little, and many differences are inherited. Those whose traits suit the place best tend to survive and have more young, and the young inherit those traits. Over many generations the helpful trait becomes common. No animal grows a trait because it needs one; the trait was already in the population.

blocks.title: Match it
blocks.q: How does a heron's long legs help it?
steps: Herons hunt fish in shallow water.
Long legs let them wade without getting their bodies wet.
blocks.a: They let it wade in to hunt.

blocks.title: Explain it
blocks.q: How did giraffes come to have long necks?
steps: Giraffes varied in neck length.
Those with longer necks reached more leaves, survived better and had more young.
Over many generations long necks became common.
blocks.a: Through inherited differences and survival over many generations.

blocks.html: Thinking an animal grows an adaptation because it needs it ("the giraffe stretched its neck, so its young had longer necks"). Changes made during one life are not inherited. Adaptations are inherited traits that were already in the population and became common.

blocks.html: Adaptations are not only body parts. What an animal does helps it survive too.

An instinct is a behavior an animal does right the first time without learning, like a spider spinning a web. A learned behavior comes from experience, practice or watching others, like a crow learning which trash cans hold food.

blocks.name: bi-classify

cards.text: A spider spins its first web
A newly hatched sea turtle crawls to the ocean
A crow finds which trash cans hold food
A young chimpanzee fishes for termites with a stick, after watching adults
cards.why: Young chimpanzees learn this by watching and practicing.

blocks.cap: Instinct or learned?

blocks.html: Instincts are inherited, built in by an animal's genes, so they work the first time, with no teacher. That matters when there is no time to learn: a sea turtle hatchling has no parent to show it the way to the sea. Learned behavior lets an animal adjust to its own surroundings, but it is not passed on in genes: each animal must learn it again.

blocks.title: Sort it
blocks.q: A honeybee does a dance that shows other bees where flowers are. Instinct or learned?
steps: Bees do this dance without being taught.

blocks.title: Passed on?
blocks.q: A dog learns to open a door latch. Will its puppies know how without being taught?
steps: Learned behavior is not stored in genes.
The puppies might learn it by watching, but they are not born knowing it.

blocks.html: Thinking animals do everything by instinct, or that learned behavior is passed to offspring through genes. Many animals learn a great deal, and what they learn must be learned again by each young animal. Watch birds at a feeder and see how they figure out a new feeder over a few days; Nature Study has more to try.

sources.name: OpenStax, Biology 2e, 45.7 Behavioral Biology: Proximate and Ultimate Causes of Behavior

blocks.html: In Vertebrate Groups the table had a column for body temperature. Here is what it means.

Birds and mammals are endotherms: they make heat inside their bodies and keep a fairly steady temperature. Fish, amphibians and reptiles (and most invertebrates) are ectotherms: their temperature follows their surroundings.

blocks.name: bi-chart
blocks.cap: Body temperature against air temperature for a mouse and a lizard (rounded example values).

blocks.html: Making heat costs energy, and energy comes from food. So a mouse needs much more food for its size than a lizard does. In return, the mouse stays active on a cold night. A lizard warms itself by basking in the sun and cools off in the shade or a burrow, and it slows down when it is cold.

blocks.title: Read the chart
blocks.q: At an air temperature of 10 °C, about how warm is each animal?
steps: The mouse line stays at about 37 °C.
The lizard line is at about 12 °C, near the air temperature.

blocks.title: Which is which?
blocks.q: A frog's body temperature rises from 10 °C to 25 °C as a pond warms. Endotherm or ectotherm?
steps: Its temperature follows its surroundings.

blocks.html: Thinking "cold-blooded" animals have cold blood. A lizard basking in the sun can be as warm as a person, or warmer; its temperature simply depends on its surroundings. Scientists prefer the word "ectotherm."

blocks.html: In The Characteristics of Life you learned how to tell whether something is alive. Now zoom out to a whole pond, forest or field. Ecologists split every place into two kinds of parts and then ask how the parts affect each other.
An ecosystem is all the biotic (living or once-living) parts of a place together with its abiotic (never-living) parts: sunlight, water, air, soil minerals, rock and temperature.

blocks.name: bi-classify

cards.why: Sunlight is energy, not a living thing.
A rotting log was part of a tree. It is food for fungi and insects, so it belongs to the biotic world.
A fallen leaf is once-living matter that decomposers will break down.

opts.prompt: Tap a card, then a group. Watch out for the once-living things.

blocks.cap: Sort the parts of a pond-side ecosystem.

blocks.html: The prefix bio- means life and a- means without. Dead leaves, a log or a bone are made of matter that living things built, and that matter still feeds decomposers. That is why ecologists count them as biotic. Abiotic parts were never alive.
The two kinds of parts work on each other. Water and temperature decide which plants can grow. Plants shade the ground, hold soil in place and add oxygen to the air. Earthworms mix the soil.

blocks.title: Sort a forest floor
blocks.q: A hiker lists: moss, a granite boulder, rainwater, a fallen pine cone, a beetle, the shade under the trees. Which are biotic?
steps: Moss and the beetle are alive now: biotic.
The pine cone grew on a pine tree. It is once-living: biotic.
The boulder and the rainwater were never alive: abiotic.
Shade is less sunlight reaching the ground, so it is an abiotic condition (even though trees cause it).
blocks.a: Biotic: moss, pine cone, beetle. Abiotic: boulder, rainwater, shade.

blocks.html: Many students put dead leaves, logs and bones with the abiotic parts because they are not alive now. Ask one question instead: was it ever part of a living thing? If yes, it is biotic. Abiotic means never living, like rock, water, sunlight and air.

sources.name: Next Generation Science Standards, MS-LS2-1 (Ecosystems: Interactions, Energy, and Dynamics)

OpenStax, Concepts of Biology, 20.1 Energy Flow through Ecosystems

blocks.html: Ecologists study life at different sizes, the way a map can show one street or a whole state. Each level adds something to the one below it. You already know the biotic and abiotic parts from Living and Nonliving Parts.
Organism: one living thing. Population: all the members of one species in an area. Community: all the populations of different species living there. Ecosystem: the community plus the abiotic parts.

head: Level
In a pond
What it adds
rows: all the bluegills in the pond
the community plus water, mud, sunlight
all freshwater lakes and ponds with similar conditions
blocks.cap: Levels from small to large.

blocks.html: A population matters because its members can breed with each other and compete for exactly the same food and space. That is why the word is kept for one species. Different species in the same place interact in other ways, as predators, prey and partners, so together they get a different name: the community.

blocks.name: bi-classify

cards.text: All the red foxes in a valley
The foxes, rabbits, grasses and hawks of the valley
cards.why: Many species together is a community.

cards.text: The valley's living things plus its stream, soil and weather
All the frogs, fish and insects in a pond
cards.why: Frogs, fish and insects are different species, so this is a community, not a population.

cards.text: The oak trees in a park

blocks.cap: Which level is each one?

blocks.title: Population or community?
blocks.q: A student writes: "The animals in the pond are a population." Is that right?
steps: How many species are named? The animals of a pond include frogs, fish, snails and insects: several species.
A population has only one species.
Several species living together form a community (and plants and microbes belong to the community too).
blocks.a: No. The animals of a pond are part of a community. "All the green frogs in the pond" would be a population.

blocks.html: Students call all the animals in a pond a population. A population is always one species. Check by asking: could I name these with one species name? If you need several names, it is a community.

OpenStax, Concepts of Biology, 19.4 Community Ecology

blocks.html: Every organism in an ecosystem gets energy and matter somehow. In Photosynthesis you saw plants make sugar from carbon dioxide and water using light. That one trick sorts all of life into three roles.

Producers make their own food, mostly by photosynthesis (plants, algae, some bacteria). Consumers eat other organisms: herbivores eat producers, carnivores eat animals, omnivores eat both. Decomposers (fungi, many bacteria) break down dead matter and wastes and return nutrients to the soil and water.

blocks.name: bi-foodweb
blocks.cap: A meadow, colored by role. The decomposers take in dead matter from every level.

blocks.html: Matter has to be reused. A meadow has only so much nitrogen and phosphorus. When a fox dies or a leaf falls, those nutrients are locked inside. Decomposers digest the dead matter and release the nutrients in simple forms that plant roots can take up again. Without them, producers would run out of nutrients and everything that eats producers would follow.

blocks.title: Name the role
blocks.q: A mushroom grows on a rotting stump. A deer eats clover. A hawk eats a snake. What role does each play?
steps: The mushroom feeds on dead wood and breaks it down: a decomposer.
The deer eats a producer: a consumer (a herbivore).
The hawk eats an animal: a consumer (a carnivore).
The clover makes its own food from sunlight: a producer.
blocks.a: Mushroom: decomposer. Deer and hawk: consumers. Clover: producer.

blocks.title: A tricky one
blocks.q: Is an earthworm eating dead leaves in the soil a consumer or a decomposer?
steps: It feeds on dead plant matter and wastes, not on living things.
Ecologists group animals like earthworms, which break down dead matter, with the decomposers (they are sometimes called detritivores).

blocks.html: Students leave decomposers out of an ecosystem, or think they are just consumers that eat living things. Decomposers feed on dead matter and wastes from every level. Check any food web you draw: is there a decomposer that receives matter from the plants and the animals?

sources.name: Next Generation Science Standards, MS-LS2-3 (Ecosystems: Interactions, Energy, and Dynamics)

OpenStax, Concepts of Biology, 13.3 Fungi (fungi as decomposers)

blocks.html: A food chain follows energy along one path: grass → rabbit → fox. Real ecosystems are messier. A rabbit is eaten by foxes and hawks, and a fox eats mice and rabbits. Link all the chains together and you get a food web. The roles come from Producers, Consumers and Decomposers.
In food chains and webs, the arrow points from the food to the eater. It shows the direction energy and matter move: grass → rabbit means the rabbit eats the grass.

blocks.name: bi-foodweb
blocks.cap: Tap any species to light up what it eats and what eats it.

blocks.html: Read every arrow as "is eaten by" or "gives energy to." Energy enters from the sun into the producers, so every arrow path starts at a producer and points up toward the top predators. If the arrows pointed the other way, energy would flow from the fox into the grass, which never happens.

blocks.title: Count the chains
blocks.q: In the meadow web, how many food chains end at the fox?
steps: The fox eats mice and rabbits.
Chains to the fox through the rabbit: grass → rabbit → fox. That is 1.
Chains through the mouse: grass → mouse → fox, and grass → grasshopper → mouse → fox, and flower → grasshopper → mouse → fox. That is 3.
Total: 1 + 3.
blocks.a: 4 food chains end at the fox.

blocks.title: Trophic levels
blocks.q: In the chain grass → grasshopper → robin → hawk, which level is the robin?
steps: Producers are level 1: grass.
Primary consumers (herbivores) are level 2: the grasshopper.
Secondary consumers are level 3: the robin.
blocks.a: The robin is a secondary consumer (level 3).

blocks.html: Students draw the arrows from the eater to the food, as if the arrow meant "eats." Then "fox → rabbit" looks right but is backward. Check: does your arrow path start at a plant or alga? Energy always starts with producers.

sources.name: Next Generation Science Standards, MS-LS2-3 (Ecosystems: Interactions, Energy, and Dynamics)

Grokipedia, "Food web"

blocks.html: Because a food web links many species, a change to one population travels along the arrows. Ecologists predict these ripples, and then check them against data.
When one population grows or shrinks, the species that eat it and the species it eats change too, and then the species linked to those change. Effects can reach plants two or three steps away.

blocks.name: bi-foodweb
blocks.cap: Tap a species to remove it. ▲ and ▼ show the first effects on its neighbors.

blocks.html: Follow the energy. If foxes disappear from a meadow, fewer rabbits are eaten, so the rabbit population grows. More rabbits eat more grass, so the grass shrinks. Later, with too little grass, the rabbits run short of food and their numbers fall again. Every step is just "more eaters means less food" or "fewer eaters means more food."

blocks.title: Lose the frogs
blocks.q: In a pond, herons eat frogs and fish. Frogs eat insects. What could happen if a disease wiped out the frogs?
steps: Frogs eat insects, so with no frogs, more insects survive: insects ▲.
Herons lose one of their foods, so they eat more fish: fish ▼, or herons may leave or decline.
Insects that eat plants or algae may then reduce those producers.
blocks.a: Insects increase; herons eat more fish (fish decrease) or herons decline; the producers the insects eat may decrease.

blocks.html: A real case: gray wolves were missing from Yellowstone National Park for decades, and 31 wolves were brought back in 1995 and 1996. Elk changed where and how they fed. Ecologists still debate how much this helped willows and aspens recover, because drought, other predators and people also affect the elk and the plants.

Students think removing a predator affects only its prey. Trace at least two steps: predator → prey → the prey's food. Also look sideways: other predators of that prey, and other foods of the predator, change too.

sources.name: Next Generation Science Standards, MS-LS2-4 (Ecosystems: Interactions, Energy, and Dynamics)
OpenStax, Concepts of Biology, 19.4 Community Ecology
National Park Service, Wolf Restoration, Yellowstone National Park
Grokipedia, "History of wolves in Yellowstone" (the debate over the size of the effects)

blocks.html: Each arrow in a food web carries energy. How much? Ecologists measure it in kilocalories (kcal) per square meter per year, and the numbers shrink fast as you climb. You will use percents of a number.

About 10% of the energy at one level is stored in the bodies of the next level. The other 90% is used to live (moving, keeping warm, growing) and leaves as heat, or is never eaten or digested. Energy flows one way; it does not cycle.

blocks.name: bi-pyramid
blocks.cap: An energy pyramid. Drag the slider to change the share passed up.

blocks.html: A mouse eats a grasshopper, but most of the grasshopper's energy was already spent: it powered hopping and chewing and escaped as heat. Only the energy stored in the grasshopper's body can pass on. This is why a field supports millions of grass plants, thousands of grasshoppers and only a few hawks.

blocks.title: Climb the pyramid
blocks.q: Grass in a field stores 20,000 kcal. With about 10% passed up each step, how much reaches the snakes in grass → grasshopper → mouse → snake?
steps: Grasshoppers: 10% of 20,000 = 2,000 kcal.
Mice: 10% of 2,000 = 200 kcal.
Snakes: 10% of 200 = 20 kcal.

blocks.title: Work backward
blocks.q: Hawks at level 4 get 15 kcal. About how much energy did the producers store?
steps: Each step down multiplies by 10.
Level 3: 150 kcal. Level 2: 1,500 kcal. Level 1: 15,000 kcal.

blocks.html: Students think energy is recycled like matter, or that each level passes on all its energy. Matter (carbon, nitrogen) cycles. Energy enters as sunlight, flows up, and leaves as heat at every step. Check: the numbers in an energy pyramid must get smaller going up.
The 10% figure is a rule of thumb. Real transfers range from about 5% to 20%, depending on the organisms.

blocks.html: Food webs show who eats whom. But species meet in other ways too. Ecologists name each relationship by asking a simple question: does each species gain (+), lose (−) or stay about the same (0)? It builds on Food Chains and Food Webs.

head: Relationship
Effect
Example
rows: Lions and hyenas competing for the same zebras; two kinds of plants competing for light
An owl catches and eats a mouse
Bees get nectar; the flowers get pollinated
Barnacles ride on a whale and reach food; the whale is barely affected
A tick feeds on a deer's blood for days; the deer is harmed but not killed right away
blocks.cap: Interactions, scored for each species.

blocks.html: Symbiosis means two species living closely together for a long time. It comes in three kinds: mutualism (both benefit), commensalism (one benefits, the other is unaffected) and parasitism (one benefits, the host is harmed).

blocks.name: bi-classify

cards.text: Tapeworms live in a dog's gut
cards.why: The tapeworm feeds for a long time; the dog is harmed.

cards.text: Clownfish shelter in an anemone and help keep it clean
Two bird species eat the same seeds
A bird nests in a tree
cards.why: The bird gains a home; the tree is not helped or hurt.

cards.text: Bacteria in cow stomachs digest grass, and the cow feeds them

blocks.cap: Sort each pair.

blocks.html: Predation and parasitism both have the pattern + / −, so the difference is in time and size. A predator kills and eats its prey, usually quickly. A parasite is usually much smaller than its host and lives on or in it for a long time, feeding without killing it right away. A dead host would end the parasite's food supply.

blocks.title: Name it
blocks.q: A flea lives in a dog's fur and feeds on its blood for weeks. A wolf kills and eats a rabbit. Which one is predation?
steps: Score each pair: flea + / dog −; wolf + / rabbit −. Both are + / −.
The wolf kills and eats the rabbit in one meal: predation.
The flea feeds on a living host over a long time without killing it: parasitism.
blocks.a: The wolf and the rabbit. The flea is a parasite.

blocks.html: Students call every close relationship helpful, or call predation parasitism. Score both sides with +, − or 0 first. If one side is harmed, it is not mutualism. If the harmed one is killed and eaten, it is predation; if it is fed on over time, it is parasitism.

blocks.html: In Photosynthesis and Respiration Together you saw that photosynthesis and respiration run in opposite directions. Follow one carbon atom through an ecosystem and you will see those two processes driving a loop.

Carbon moves from the air (as carbon dioxide) into plants by photosynthesis, into animals by eating, and back to the air by respiration, decomposition and burning. Some carbon is stored for a long time in oceans, rock and fossil fuels.

blocks.name: bi-cycle
blocks.cap: The carbon cycle. Tap an arrow to read the process. The dots are carbon atoms on the move.

blocks.html: Atoms are never used up. When you digest a sandwich, its carbon atoms do not vanish: your cells break the sugar apart in respiration and you breathe the carbon out as carbon dioxide. A plant can take that same carbon dioxide in and build it into a new leaf. Matter cycles; only the energy is spent.

blocks.title: Follow an atom
blocks.q: A carbon atom is in the air. Name a path that brings it back to the air through a deer.
steps: Photosynthesis: a clover plant takes in the carbon dioxide and builds sugar.
Eating: a deer eats the clover.
Respiration: the deer's cells break down the sugar and release carbon dioxide, which the deer breathes out.

blocks.title: The slow route
blocks.q: How can carbon stay out of the air for millions of years?
steps: Dead plants and animals can be buried before they fully decompose.
Over millions of years, heat and pressure turn some of them into coal, oil or natural gas (fossil fuels).
Burning those fuels returns the carbon to the air quickly.
blocks.a: Burial as fossil fuels (and as rock and in the deep ocean) stores carbon for a very long time.

blocks.html: Students think the carbon in food disappears when it is used, or that respiration makes energy out of nothing. The atoms remain; respiration rearranges them into carbon dioxide and water and releases the energy that was stored in the bonds.

sources.name: Next Generation Science Standards, MS-LS2-3 (Ecosystems: Interactions, Energy, and Dynamics)
