Grokipedia, "Carbon cycle"

blocks.html: Living things need nitrogen to build proteins and DNA. Air is about 78% nitrogen gas, so it seems easy. But nitrogen gas (N₂) has two atoms held by a very strong triple bond, and plants and animals cannot break it. This is where the Bacteria come in. Compare it with the The Carbon Cycle.

Nitrogen-fixing bacteria in soil and in the root nodules of plants such as peas, beans and clover turn N₂ into ammonium and nitrates that roots can absorb. Animals get nitrogen by eating plants. Decomposers return nitrogen from dead matter and wastes to the soil, and denitrifying bacteria return it to the air.

blocks.name: bi-cycle
blocks.cap: The nitrogen cycle. Tap each arrow: most of the steps are done by bacteria.

blocks.html: Breaking the triple bond takes a special enzyme that only certain microbes, mostly bacteria, have. A bean plant gives its root-nodule bacteria sugar; the bacteria give the plant usable nitrogen. That mutualism is why farmers plant beans or clover to enrich soil. Lightning fixes a small amount of nitrogen too.

blocks.title: Why the nodules?
blocks.q: Two bean plants grow in nitrogen-poor soil. One has root nodules with bacteria; one has none. Which grows better, and why?
steps: Neither plant can use nitrogen gas from the air directly.
The bacteria in the nodules fix N₂ into ammonium the plant can use.
The plant without nodules depends on the little nitrogen already in the soil.
blocks.a: The plant with nodules, because its bacteria supply usable nitrogen.

blocks.title: Back to the soil
blocks.q: A rabbit dies in a meadow. How does its nitrogen get back to the grass?
steps: The rabbit's proteins hold nitrogen.
Decomposers break the proteins down and release ammonium into the soil.
Grass roots absorb it (often after other bacteria turn it into nitrate).
blocks.a: Decomposition returns it to the soil as ammonium; roots take it up.

blocks.html: Students think plants take nitrogen from the air through their leaves, the way they take in carbon dioxide. Leaves can't use N₂. Plants get nitrogen through their roots, as ammonium or nitrate, thanks to bacteria.

blocks.html: Fly across North America and you pass desert, grassland, forest and frozen tundra. Ecologists group the world's ecosystems into biomes. The question is what decides where each one is. Start from the abiotic parts in Living and Nonliving Parts.

A biome is a large region with a similar climate (temperature and yearly rainfall) and similar kinds of plants and animals. Climate decides the plants, and the plants decide which animals can live there.

head: Biome
Rain per year (about)
Temperature
Plants
rows: shrubs and other plants that store or save water (cactuses in the Americas)
hot summers, cold or mild winters
trees that drop leaves in fall
blocks.cap: The six land biomes in this course (rounded ranges).

blocks.name: bi-chart
blocks.cap: Rainfall drops from rainforest to desert. Temperature separates tundra from desert, which both get little rain.

blocks.html: Plants are rooted in place, so they must survive the local climate all year. Tall broadleaf trees need lots of water. Grasses survive drought and fire because they grow from the base. Conifers' needles handle snow and short summers. Animals follow their food and shelter, so they match the plants.

blocks.title: Name the biome
blocks.q: A place gets about 15 cm of rain a year, the ground is frozen most of the year, and the plants are mosses and lichens. Which biome?
steps: 15 cm is very little rain: desert or tundra.
Frozen ground and mosses and lichens mean very cold.

blocks.html: Students define biomes by place names ("the Sahara") or by animals ("where camels live"). A biome is defined by temperature and rainfall. Deserts exist on several continents with different animals, and they are all deserts because they are dry.

blocks.cap: The taiga: evergreen conifers and long winters.

blocks.html: Ecosystems are not frozen. After a fire, a flood, a volcano or an abandoned farm field, the community rebuilds in stages. This change over time is ecological succession, and the climate of the biome decides where it ends up.

Primary succession starts where there is no soil, as on new lava rock or ground left bare by a glacier. Secondary succession starts where soil remains after a disturbance, as after a forest fire or on an abandoned field. Secondary succession is faster.

blocks.name: bi-feedback

steps: Bare rock: no soil
Pioneer species: lichens and mosses break rock into thin soil
Grasses and small plants
Shrubs
Fast-growing sun-loving trees
A mature forest
opts.title: Primary succession on bare rock

blocks.cap: The stages of primary succession. Each stage changes the conditions for the next.

blocks.html: Each stage prepares the ground for the next. Lichens grip bare rock and release acids that crumble it; when they die they add organic matter, and a thin soil starts. Mosses and grasses can then root, adding more soil and holding water. Taller plants shade out the early ones. After a fire, the soil, seeds and roots are already there, so recovery skips the slow soil-making stages.

blocks.title: Which kind?
blocks.q: Compare two places: land buried under fresh volcanic rock by the 1980 eruption of Mount St. Helens, and a forest that burns in a wildfire but keeps its soil. Which shows primary succession?
steps: Fresh volcanic rock has no soil: life must start almost from scratch.
The burned forest kept its soil, seeds and roots.
blocks.a: The fresh volcanic rock shows primary succession; the burned forest shows secondary succession.

blocks.html: Students think succession always starts from bare rock, or that an ecosystem stays the same forever once it forms. Ask: is there soil? If yes, it is secondary succession, and it is faster. Even mature forests keep changing with storms, fires and new species.
Glacier Bay in Alaska is a classic study site: as the glacier melted back over about 200 years, it left a row of sites of different ages, from bare ground with mosses to spruce and hemlock forest.

blocks.html: Biodiversity is the variety of life: the number of different species, the genetic differences within each species, and the variety of ecosystems. You have met the ways species depend on each other in Competition, Predation and Symbiosis and how communities rebuild in Ecological Succession.

Biodiversity counts kinds, not individuals. Healthy ecosystems provide ecosystem services people rely on: clean water, fertile soil, pollination of crops, food, wood and medicines. More diverse ecosystems often recover better after a disturbance.

blocks.name: bi-chart

opts.title: Three sample plots (made-up numbers for practice)

blocks.cap: The lawn has the most plants but the fewest species: low biodiversity.

blocks.html: Diversity spreads the risk. If a disease kills one kind of grass in a prairie with thirty species, other plants fill the gap and the animals that need plants still have food. In a field of a single crop, the same disease can wipe out everything at once. Many species also do overlapping jobs, like pollinating or holding soil, so losing one does not stop the job.

blocks.title: Compare two plots
blocks.q: Plot A has 500 plants of 3 species. Plot B has 300 plants of 12 species. Which has greater species diversity?
steps: Count kinds, not individuals.
Plot A: 3 species. Plot B: 12 species.
blocks.a: Plot B, even though it has fewer plants.

blocks.title: Name the service
blocks.q: Honeybees and wild bees visit apple blossoms. What ecosystem service is that?
steps: Apple trees need pollen moved from flower to flower to make apples.
The bees do that work for free.

blocks.html: Students measure biodiversity by the number of individuals. A field with a thousand plants of one kind has very low diversity. Always ask: how many different species are there, and is any one species taking over?

Grokipedia, "Biodiversity"

blocks.html: People are part of ecosystems too. We farm, build, fish, travel and use water and energy, and these choices change the Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services around us. Ecologists sort the main threats into a few kinds, and engineers and communities compare ways to reduce them.

The main threats to ecosystems are habitat loss, invasive species, pollution and overharvesting (taking fish, animals or plants faster than they can be replaced). Solutions such as protected areas, cleanup, controls on invasive species and harvest limits each have costs and benefits that people weigh.

blocks.name: bi-classify

cards.text: A wetland is drained and paved for a parking lot
Zebra mussels arrive in the Great Lakes in ships' ballast water
Fertilizer washes off fields into a lake and feeds huge algae blooms
A fishing fleet catches cod faster than they can reproduce
A forest is cleared for new houses

blocks.cap: Sort each example by the kind of threat.

blocks.html: Each threat breaks a link you already know. Habitat loss removes food and shelter, so populations fall below what they need. An invasive species arrives without the predators, parasites or competitors that held it in check at home, so it spreads and crowds out natives. Pollution changes the abiotic parts. Overharvesting removes individuals faster than births can replace them.

blocks.title: An invader
blocks.q: Zebra mussels were first found in North America in 1988, in Lake St. Clair, carried from Europe in ships' ballast water. Why can a new species spread so fast?
steps: In its new home it has few predators and parasites that evolved to eat it.
It competes with native species for food and space.
Its population grows until food and space run short.
blocks.a: It escapes the predators and diseases of its home range, so little holds it back at first.

blocks.html: Students think any change people make harms nature, or that nature always fixes itself. Effects depend on the change: a well-managed fishery can last for generations, while an untreated spill can kill a river. Good solutions are compared by what they cost, what they protect and who they affect, and people can weigh those differently.

blocks.html: A population is all the members of one species in an area. Its size changes in only four ways: individuals are born, arrive, die or leave. Keep track of those four numbers and you can predict the next count.

Change in a population = (births + arrivals) − (deaths + departures). With plenty of food and space, each individual adds offspring, so a larger population adds more each year: the growth itself grows. Graphed, this exponential growth makes a J-shaped curve.

blocks.title: Count the changes
blocks.q: A herd of 200 deer has 60 fawns born in a year. 15 deer arrive from a nearby forest, 35 die and 10 leave. How many deer are there at the end of the year?

blocks.html: Imagine pond plants that double every week. Start with 10. After one week there are 20 (10 added), then 40 (20 added), then 80 (40 added). The number added each week doubles too, because every plant makes new ones. That is why unchecked growth starts slowly and then shoots up.

blocks.name: bi-population
blocks.cap: Bacteria doubling each generation: 1, 2, 4, 8 … The added amount grows each time.

blocks.title: Growth that grows
blocks.q: A population of 100 mice grows by 50% each year while food is plentiful. How many mice after 2 years?
steps: Notice the gain went from 50 to 75.

blocks.name: bi-population
blocks.cap: Exponential growth: the J-curve. Drag the growth rate.

blocks.html: Students think a population grows by the same number each year, like adding 50 every time. That is only true when the number of new births stays fixed. When each individual adds offspring, the gain grows with the population. Check: compare the gains from one year to the next. If they grow, the growth is exponential.

sources.name: Next Generation Science Standards, MS-LS2-1 (Ecosystems: Interactions, Energy, and Dynamics)
OpenStax, Concepts of Biology, 19.2 Population Growth and Regulation (exponential growth)

blocks.html: No population keeps a J-curve for long. In How Populations Grow food and space were plentiful. Sooner or later something runs short.

A limiting factor is anything that keeps a population from growing: food, water, space, shelter, light, disease, predators. The largest population an environment can support over time is its carrying capacity (K). A population growing toward K follows an S-shaped curve and then rises and falls around K.

blocks.name: bi-population
blocks.cap: J-curve and S-curve. Change K and watch where the S-curve levels off.

blocks.html: When a population is small, each individual finds plenty of food, so births beat deaths. As the population nears K, each individual gets less: more go hungry, disease spreads more easily in crowds, and fewer young survive. Births and deaths come into balance. If a good year pushes the population above K, food runs short and it drops back.

blocks.title: Which factor limits?
blocks.q: A pond has plenty of insects for its frogs and lots of water, but only a few logs and rocks where frogs can hide from herons. What limits the frog population?
steps: Food: plenty. Water: plenty.
Shelter: scarce. Frogs without cover are caught by herons.
blocks.a: Shelter (and the herons that catch unsheltered frogs).

blocks.title: Read the curve
blocks.q: A deer population grows from 50 to 400 in eight years, then stays between 380 and 420 for the next ten years. About what is the carrying capacity?
steps: The population stops growing and moves up and down around one level.
The middle of 380 to 420 is 400.

blocks.html: Students think a population sits exactly at carrying capacity, or that one plentiful resource lets it grow forever. Plenty of food does not help if there is no water or shelter: whatever runs short first sets the limit. And real populations rise and fall around K from year to year.
Carrying capacity can change. A wet year grows more grass, so a meadow can feed more rabbits; a drought lowers K.

blocks.html: Predators are a limiting factor for their prey, and prey are food, a limiting factor, for predators. So the two populations are tied together, as you saw in Limiting Factors and Carrying Capacity and Food Chains and Food Webs.

When prey are plentiful, predators eat well and their numbers rise. More predators eat more prey, so the prey fall. With less food, predators fall next. With fewer predators, the prey recover. The two populations rise and fall in turns, and the predator peak comes after the prey peak.

blocks.name: bi-population
blocks.cap: Prey (green) and predators (red). Find each predator peak and the prey peak just before it.

blocks.html: Predators need time to respond. A fox that eats well this year raises more kits, but those kits hunt only later. So the predator count keeps climbing for a while after the prey begin to fall, and keeps falling for a while after the prey start to recover. That delay is the lag between the curves.

blocks.title: Read the lag
blocks.q: In a graph of snowshoe hares and lynx, the hares peak in year 4 and again in year 14. The lynx peak in years 6 and 16. How long is the lag?
steps: The lynx peak comes after each hare peak.
6 − 4 = 2 years; 16 − 14 = 2 years.

blocks.title: Predict the next step
blocks.q: Prey numbers are falling fast and predator numbers are at their highest. What happens next?
steps: Fewer prey means less food for each predator.
Fewer predator young survive, and some predators starve or leave.
blocks.a: The predator population starts to fall.

blocks.html: Students think predators wipe out their prey, or that both populations peak at the same time. Predators usually cannot catch the last few prey, which hide or spread out, and starving predators decline first. On a graph, find the prey peak, then look a little later for the predator peak.
Try it in the Predators and Prey lab: change the number of foxes and rabbits and watch the cycles form.
A famous data set comes from fur-trading records in Canada, which show snowshoe hare and lynx numbers rising and falling for about a century. The hares' food supply plays a part in the cycle too.

blocks.html: Nobody can count every dandelion in a park. Ecologists count a few small sample squares, called quadrats, and scale up. It is the same thinking as a unit rate: find the count per square meter, then multiply by the number of square meters.
Estimate = average count per quadrat × (total area ÷ area of one quadrat). Use several quadrats placed at random, and make sure both areas use the same units.

blocks.name: lifesci-quadrat
blocks.cap: A field split into 60 quadrats of 1 m² each. Tap squares to sample them and watch the estimate change.

blocks.html: Plants are not spread evenly. One quadrat might land on a bare patch and another on a thick clump. Averaging several random quadrats cancels out lucky and unlucky squares, so the estimate gets closer to the truth. Random placement keeps you from choosing only the thick patches.

blocks.title: Scale up
blocks.q: Five 1 m² quadrats in a 200 m² meadow hold 4, 7, 3, 6 and 5 clover plants. Estimate the clover population.
steps: Average: (4 + 7 + 3 + 6 + 5) ÷ 5 = 25 ÷ 5 = 5 plants per quadrat.
Quadrats in the meadow: 200 m² ÷ 1 m² = 200.

blocks.title: Match the units
blocks.q: Quadrats are 0.5 m on each side and hold an average of 3 snails. The garden is 20 m². How many snails?
steps: Area of one quadrat: 0.5 m × 0.5 m = 0.25 m².
Number of quadrats that fit: 20 ÷ 0.25 = 80.
Estimate: 3 × 80 = 240.

blocks.html: Two mistakes are common. Some students multiply one quadrat's count by the whole area without averaging several. Others forget to match units: a quadrat 50 cm on a side is 0.25 m², not 50 m² or 0.5 m². Check: does your estimate equal (average per m²) × (area in m²)?
Animals that move around are counted other ways, such as catching, marking and releasing some, then seeing what share of a later catch is marked.

blocks.html: In Cells, Tissues, Organs and Systems you saw cells build tissues, tissues build organs, and organs work together as organ systems. The first system to meet is the frame that holds the rest of you up.

The skeleton has four jobs: it supports the body, protects organs (the skull guards the brain, the ribs guard the heart and lungs), works with muscles to let you move, and makes blood cells in the marrow inside many bones. An adult skeleton usually has 206 bones.

blocks.name: bi-body
blocks.cap: The skeletal system. Tap a bone to name it, or switch to another system.

blocks.html: Bone is a living organ. It has bone cells, blood vessels and nerves, and it stores calcium the body can draw on. Bone cells keep removing old bone and building new bone. That is how bones grow longer in children, get stronger with use, and knit back together after a break, usually with a cast or splint holding the pieces still.

blocks.title: Match the job
blocks.q: Which job does each bone mainly do? (a) the skull (b) the femur, the thigh bone (c) the ribs
steps: The skull surrounds the brain: protection.
The femur holds up your weight and is pulled by thigh muscles when you walk: support and movement.
The ribs wrap the heart and lungs: protection (and they move when you breathe).

blocks.title: Where blood cells come from
blocks.q: A doctor studies red marrow. What is it making?
steps: Red marrow is the soft tissue inside many bones, such as the hips and ribs.
It makes red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets.

blocks.html: Students think bones are dead, dry sticks, like the white skeletons in a museum. Those are only the mineral part left behind. In a living body bones are alive: they grow, repair themselves after breaks, and make blood cells.
Babies are born with more separate bone pieces than adults. Many of them fuse together as a child grows, which is part of why the adult count is 206.

blocks.html: Bones cannot move on their own. Muscles move them, and muscles move blood and food inside you too. This builds on Bones and the Skeleton.

There are three kinds of muscle. Skeletal muscle moves bones, and you control it. Smooth muscle lines organs such as the stomach, intestines and blood vessels and works without your thinking. Cardiac muscle makes up the heart. Every muscle can only pull, by shortening, so skeletal muscles work in pairs.

blocks.name: bi-body
blocks.cap: The muscular system. Find the biceps on the front of the upper arm.

blocks.html: A muscle cell is packed with protein fibers that slide past each other and shorten the cell. They cannot push it longer. So to bend your elbow, the biceps on the front of the upper arm shortens and pulls the forearm up. To straighten it again, the triceps on the back shortens and pulls the other way while the biceps relaxes and is stretched.

blocks.title: Which muscle pulls?
blocks.q: You kick a ball by straightening your knee. The quadriceps are on the front of the thigh and the hamstrings on the back. Which muscle group shortens to straighten the knee?
steps: Straightening the knee swings the lower leg forward.
The quadriceps, on the front, attach below the knee and pull the lower leg forward.
The hamstrings relax and are stretched.

blocks.title: Name the kind
blocks.q: Food is squeezed along your intestines while you sleep. What kind of muscle does that?
steps: It works without your control.
It lines an organ, not a bone.

blocks.html: Students think a muscle pushes to straighten a joint. Muscles only shorten and pull. When a joint straightens, look for the muscle on the opposite side doing the pulling: the triceps straightens the elbow while the biceps relaxes.

sources.name: Next Generation Science Standards, MS-LS1-3 (From Molecules to Organisms: Structures and Processes)
OpenStax, Concepts of Biology, 16.5 Musculoskeletal System (skeletal muscle and antagonistic pairs)

blocks.html: Your cells need small molecules: simple sugars, amino acids and fatty acids. A sandwich is made of big molecules. The digestive system is a long tube that breaks food down and lets those small molecules into the blood. Its organs are a good example of Cells, Tissues, Organs and Systems.

Food travels mouth → esophagus → stomach → small intestine → large intestine. Teeth and the stomach break food into pieces; enzymes break the pieces into small molecules. Most nutrients are absorbed in the small intestine. The large intestine absorbs water.

blocks.name: bi-body
blocks.cap: Step along the path food takes. The liver is beside the path, not on it.

blocks.html: Digestion has two parts. Mechanical digestion (chewing, the stomach churning) makes pieces smaller, so enzymes have more surface to work on. Chemical digestion uses enzymes: saliva starts breaking starch in your mouth, the stomach starts on proteins with acid and enzymes, and the small intestine finishes the job with enzymes from the pancreas and bile from the liver. Its inner wall is covered in tiny fingerlike folds (villi) that give a huge surface for absorbing.

blocks.title: Where does it start?
blocks.q: Chew a plain cracker for a minute and it starts to taste a little sweet. Why?
steps: Crackers are mostly starch, a chain of sugar units.
An enzyme in saliva breaks starch into smaller sugars.
blocks.a: Digestion has already started in the mouth.

blocks.title: Put it in order
blocks.q: Put these in the order food reaches them: small intestine, esophagus, large intestine, mouth, stomach.
steps: Food enters at the mouth.
It is swallowed down the esophagus into the stomach.
Then the small intestine, then the large intestine.
blocks.a: Mouth, esophagus, stomach, small intestine, large intestine.

blocks.html: Students think digestion begins in the stomach and that most absorption happens there. Digestion begins in the mouth. The stomach mixes and starts on proteins, but most nutrients pass into the blood through the walls of the small intestine.

OpenStax, Concepts of Biology, 16.2 Digestive System
National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases (NIDDK), Your Digestive System and How It Works

blocks.html: Every cell needs a delivery service: oxygen and nutrients in, carbon dioxide and wastes out. The circulatory system is that service, and its pump is made of the cardiac muscle from Muscles.

The heart pumps blood through three kinds of vessels: arteries carry blood away from the heart, capillaries are tiny vessels where materials pass between blood and cells, and veins carry blood back to the heart.

blocks.name: bi-body
blocks.cap: Step through the heart: body → right side → lungs → left side → body.

blocks.html: The heart is two pumps side by side. The right side sends oxygen-poor blood to the lungs, where it picks up oxygen and drops off carbon dioxide. The left side, with the thickest wall, pumps that oxygen-rich blood out to the whole body. Capillary walls are only one cell thick, so oxygen and nutrients can diffuse out to the cells and carbon dioxide can diffuse in.

blocks.title: Artery or vein?
blocks.q: The vessel that carries blood from the heart to the lungs carries oxygen-poor blood. Is it an artery or a vein?
steps: Arteries and veins are named by direction, not by oxygen.
This vessel carries blood away from the heart.

blocks.title: Trace the blood
blocks.q: Blood leaves a toe and returns to the toe. Name the main places it passes.
steps: Veins → right atrium → right ventricle.
Lungs (oxygen in, carbon dioxide out).
Left atrium → left ventricle → arteries → capillaries in the toe.
blocks.a: Veins, right side of the heart, lungs, left side of the heart, arteries, capillaries.

blocks.html: Students think blood in veins is blue, because diagrams color veins blue and veins look bluish through the skin. Blood is always red. Blood with less oxygen is a darker red. Veins look blue because of how skin scatters and absorbs light.

sources.name: Next Generation Science Standards, MS-LS1-3 (From Molecules to Organisms: Structures and Processes)
OpenStax, Concepts of Biology, 16.3 Circulatory and Respiratory Systems
The Conversation, "I've always wondered: why do our veins look blue when our blood is red?"

blocks.html: Your blood picks up oxygen in the lungs, as you saw in The Heart and Blood. How does air get in, and how does oxygen cross into the blood?

The diaphragm, a dome of muscle under the lungs, shortens and flattens; the chest gets bigger and air rushes in. Air travels nose → trachea → bronchi → lungs, into millions of tiny air sacs called alveoli. There oxygen diffuses into the blood and carbon dioxide diffuses out.

blocks.name: bi-body
blocks.cap: Follow the air from the nose to the lungs.

blocks.html: Gas exchange is diffusion. Air in the alveoli has more oxygen than the blood arriving from the body, so oxygen moves into the blood. That blood has more carbon dioxide than the air, so carbon dioxide moves out. The walls of the alveoli and capillaries are each one cell thick, and the alveoli give the lungs a very large surface.

head: Gas
Air breathed in
Air breathed out
blocks.cap: Approximate makeup of dry air in and air out.

blocks.name: bi-membrane
blocks.cap: Diffusion: particles spread from where they are crowded to where they are sparse, as oxygen does into the blood.

blocks.title: Read the table
blocks.q: How much of the oxygen you breathe in do you use? Use the table.
steps: In: about 21%. Out: about 16%.
Used: 21 − 16 = 5 percentage points.
As a share of what came in: 5 ÷ 21 ≈ 0.24, about a quarter.
blocks.a: About a quarter of it; most of the oxygen is breathed back out.

blocks.html: Students think we breathe in only oxygen and breathe out only carbon dioxide. Both kinds of air are mostly nitrogen. Air out still has about 16% oxygen and only about 4% carbon dioxide.

blocks.html: Touch a hot pan, and you pull your hand back before you even feel the pain. The nervous system is the body's fast message network. It is built from nerve cells, an example of cells building organs and systems.

Sense receptors (in the eyes, ears, nose, tongue and skin) detect stimuli. Nerves carry signals to the brain and spinal cord, which interpret them and decide. Nerves carry signals back out to muscles. A reflex is a fast, automatic response routed through the spinal cord.

blocks.name: bi-body
blocks.cap: The brain, spinal cord and nerves.

blocks.name: bi-feedback

steps: Receptors in the skin detect heat
A sensory nerve carries the signal to the spinal cord
The spinal cord sends a signal straight back out
A motor nerve tells the arm muscles to pull back
Signals also travel up to the brain: you feel the pain a moment later
opts.title: A reflex arc

blocks.cap: A reflex: the spinal cord answers first, and the brain hears about it after.

blocks.html: A signal takes time to travel. A short path, from the skin to the spinal cord and straight back, is faster than going all the way up to the brain and back. For dangers like heat, that saves precious time. For everything else, such as reading or catching a ball, the brain does the work: it compares signals with memory and decides.

blocks.title: Detect or decide?
blocks.q: Light from a page enters your eye, and you read the word "cat". Which part detects, and which part understands?
steps: Receptor cells at the back of the eye detect the light and send signals along the optic nerve.
The brain interprets the pattern as letters and a word.
blocks.a: The eye detects; the brain interprets.

blocks.html: Students think the eyes or hands "feel" or decide on their own. Receptors only detect and send signals; the brain interprets them. That is why the brain can be fooled: in an optical illusion the eyes send correct signals, but the brain reads them wrongly.

Grokipedia, "Reflex arc"

blocks.html: Germs are everywhere: on your hands, in the air, in food. In Helpful and Harmful Microbes you met the ones that can make us sick. Here is how the body keeps most of them out and fights the ones that get in. The fighters travel in the blood, from The Heart and Blood.

Barriers come first: skin, mucus and tiny hairs in the airways, tears and stomach acid keep most germs out. White blood cells attack germs that get in. Some white blood cells remember a germ, so the body responds faster and harder the next time it meets the same one.

blocks.name: bi-body
blocks.cap: Parts of the immune system: lymph nodes, spleen, thymus, tonsils. White blood cells travel all over the body.

blocks.html: The body has two layers of defense. The first responds the same way to any invader: barriers, then white blood cells that swallow germs, plus inflammation (swelling, redness) and sometimes fever. The second layer learns: certain white blood cells make antibodies that fit one particular germ, and memory cells keep that pattern for years. Vaccines work this way: they show the body a harmless look-alike of a germ (a weakened or killed germ, or just a piece of one) so memory forms without the illness.

blocks.title: Defense or germ?
blocks.q: You have a cold. Your nose runs and you have a mild fever. Are those the virus itself?
steps: A cold virus infects cells lining the nose and throat.
Extra mucus traps germs and washes them out; a higher temperature is part of the body's defense.
blocks.a: No. They are signs of the body's defenses at work.

blocks.title: Why faster the second time?
blocks.q: Why do people usually get chickenpox only once?
steps: During the first illness, the body makes antibodies against the chickenpox virus.
Memory cells stay in the body.
If the virus comes back, the memory cells respond before it can spread far.
blocks.a: Memory cells from the first time respond quickly.

blocks.html: Students think a fever or a runny nose is the germ itself, or that the body has only one kind of defense. Symptoms are often the body fighting back. And there are layers: barriers, the general attack, and the learned, remembering response.
Washing hands with soap and water removes many germs before they can get in (CDC). Antibiotics act on bacteria, not on viruses such as colds and flu.

OpenStax, Concepts of Biology, 17.3 Adaptive Immunity
Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, About Antimicrobial Resistance (antibiotics do not work on viruses)

blocks.html: Cells make wastes as they work, the way a kitchen makes scraps. The blood from The Heart and Blood carries those wastes away. Several organs then remove them from the body.
The kidneys filter wastes and extra water and salt from the blood and make urine, which is stored in the bladder. The lungs remove carbon dioxide. The skin releases some water and salt in sweat.

blocks.name: bi-body
blocks.cap: The kidneys, ureters and bladder.

blocks.html: When cells break down proteins, they make nitrogen wastes such as urea, which would be harmful if they built up. Each kidney contains about a million tiny filters. Blood is pushed through them, and then most of the water, sugar and salt is taken back into the blood. What is left (the wastes and extra water) becomes urine. In a day the kidneys filter about 150 quarts of blood but make only about 1 to 2 quarts of urine.

blocks.title: Which organ removes it?
blocks.q: Name the organ that removes each waste: (a) carbon dioxide from respiration (b) urea (c) extra salt on a hot day.
steps: (a) Carbon dioxide diffuses out in the alveoli and is breathed out: the lungs.
(b) Urea is filtered from the blood: the kidneys.
(c) Salt leaves in urine (kidneys) and some in sweat (skin).

blocks.title: How much is kept?
blocks.q: The kidneys filter about 150 quarts of blood a day and make about 1.5 quarts of urine. About what share of the filtered fluid is kept?
steps: Kept: 150 − 1.5 = 148.5 quarts.

blocks.html: Students think solid waste from digestion is the main waste the body makes. Most of it is food the body never absorbed, plus gut bacteria: it passed through the digestive tube without entering your cells. The wastes that cells make are carried in the blood and removed by the kidneys, lungs and skin.

OpenStax, Concepts of Biology, 16.1 Homeostasis and Osmoregulation (the kidneys)
NIDDK, Your Kidneys and How They Work

blocks.html: You have met the body's systems one at a time: breathing, the heart and blood, nerves, digestion and removing wastes. In a living body none of them works alone. Exercise shows it best.

When you run, working muscles need more oxygen and sugar and make more carbon dioxide and heat. The nervous system senses the change and speeds up breathing and the heart rate, so the blood delivers more oxygen. The skin sweats to shed heat.

blocks.name: bi-feedback

steps: Leg muscles work harder and use more oxygen
Carbon dioxide in the blood rises
The brain senses it
Breathing gets faster and deeper; the heart beats faster
More oxygen reaches the muscles and carbon dioxide is removed
Extra heat makes you sweat, cooling the skin
opts.title: Running: systems working together

blocks.cap: One activity, many systems.

blocks.html: Your cells release energy by respiration: sugar + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water + energy. Running muscles need much more energy each second, so they need more oxygen and sugar. The digestive system supplied the sugar, the respiratory system brings in oxygen, the circulatory system carries both, and the nervous system adjusts the pace of everything. Keeping conditions steady this way is called homeostasis.

blocks.name: bi-feedback
blocks.cap: Body temperature: when it rises, the brain turns on sweating until it comes back down.

blocks.title: Read the data
blocks.q: A student's heart rate is 70 beats per minute at rest and 140 after running. By how many times did it increase?

blocks.html: Students think each organ system has its own separate job and does not affect the others. During exercise, the muscular, respiratory, circulatory and nervous systems change together, and the skin joins in to cool you. Ask of any change: which other systems must respond?

blocks.html: Living things make more of their own kind, one of the The Characteristics of Life. Offspring look like their parents in some ways but not in others. To see why, first sort traits into two kinds.

An inherited trait is passed from parents to offspring through genes, like eye color, the shape of a leaf, or a dog's coat pattern. An acquired trait comes from experience or the environment during a lifetime, like a scar, a skill, a language or a pierced ear. Acquired traits are not passed on through genes.

blocks.name: bi-classify

cards.why: A language is learned from the people around you.
Training built the muscles. The weightlifter's children are not born with them.

cards.text: A dog that knows how to sit on command
The shape of a maple leaf

blocks.cap: Sort the traits.

blocks.html: Offspring get their genes from their parents' cells. Exercise, injuries and lessons change the body or the brain, but they do not change the DNA a parent passes on. So a weightlifter's child starts with ordinary muscles, and a parent who learns French has a baby who still has to learn it.

blocks.title: Sort it
blocks.q: A plant grows tall in a sunny garden. Its twin, from a cutting of the same plant, stays short in deep shade. Is the height difference inherited or acquired?
steps: The two plants have the same genes (one was grown from a piece of the other).
The difference came from the light they got.
blocks.a: Acquired: it comes from the environment.

blocks.title: Both at once
blocks.q: Height in people depends on genes and on food and health while growing up. Is height inherited or acquired?
steps: Tall parents tend to have tall children: genes matter.
A child who gets too little food may grow less than their genes allow: environment matters.
blocks.a: Both. Many traits come from genes and the environment working together.

blocks.html: Students think a skill or an injury of a parent can be inherited, such as a weightlifter's muscles or a parent's piano skill. Ask: did the trait come from genes, or was it gained during the parent's life? Only traits coded in genes are passed on.

blocks.html: In Membrane, Cytoplasm and Nucleus you saw that the nucleus is the cell's control center. What is inside it? Instructions, written in a molecule called DNA. This is where inherited traits come from.

DNA carries the instructions for building and running an organism. A gene is a section of DNA with the instructions for one protein. DNA is packed into chromosomes in the nucleus. A chromosome is one long DNA molecule carrying many genes.

blocks.name: bi-dna
blocks.cap: DNA is a double helix, like a twisted ladder. The rungs are pairs of bases: A with T, C with G.

blocks.html: The order of the bases A, T, C and G spells out the instructions, the way the order of letters spells words. Because A always pairs with T and C with G, each side of the ladder can rebuild the other. That is how a cell copies its DNA before it divides, so nearly every cell of your body has a full set.

head: Word
What it is
Size
rows: one long DNA molecule, coiled tightly
a section of a chromosome with instructions for one protein
one "letter": A, T, C or G
blocks.cap: From big to small.

blocks.title: How many?
blocks.q: Most human body cells have 46 chromosomes in 23 pairs. How many chromosomes does a skin cell have? A liver cell?
steps: Body cells are made by copying the DNA and dividing.
Each copy gets the full set.
blocks.a: Both have 46. (Red blood cells are an exception: they lose their nucleus as they mature.)

blocks.name: bi-dna
blocks.cap: Build the partner strand: A pairs with T, C pairs with G.

blocks.html: Students think genes and chromosomes are different things in different places, or that only some cells, like those in the blood, have DNA. A gene is part of a chromosome, the way a sentence is part of a book. And nearly every cell carries the whole book.

blocks.html: A gene is a recipe. But what does the recipe make, and how does that turn into a trait you can see, like brown fur?

A gene holds the instructions for one protein. Proteins do the work of the cell: some are enzymes that speed up reactions (such as making a pigment), some build structures (such as hair and muscle), and some carry things (such as hemoglobin carrying oxygen). The trait comes from what the protein does.

blocks.name: bi-central
blocks.cap: From a gene to a protein: the DNA is copied into messenger RNA, and each three-letter codon adds one amino acid.

blocks.html: Proteins are chains of building blocks called amino acids. The order of the bases in a gene sets the order of the amino acids, and that order sets the protein's shape. Shape decides the job: an enzyme's shape lets it grab one molecule and change it. Change the gene and you can change the shape, the job, and so the trait.

blocks.title: Gene to trait
blocks.q: Fur color in many mammals depends on an enzyme that helps make the dark pigment melanin. What would an animal look like if its copies of that gene made a protein that could not work?
steps: Gene → enzyme → pigment → fur color.
If the enzyme does not work, little or no dark pigment is made.
blocks.a: Very light or white fur (and often pale eyes): this is albinism.

blocks.title: Read the chain
blocks.q: In the visual, the DNA template TAC AAA CCG ATT is copied as AUG UUU GGC UAA. What does each codon mean?
steps: AUG means "start" and adds Met.
UUU adds Phe; GGC adds Gly.
UAA means "stop".

blocks.html: Students think a gene is a tiny trait, as if a "blue eye" were stored in the cell. A gene is a set of instructions for a protein. The trait appears only when the protein does its job, for example by making more or less pigment.

blocks.html: Every new organism gets its genes from its parents. But some organisms have one parent, and some have two. That one difference decides whether the offspring are copies or mixes.

One parent: a bacterium splitting in two, a yeast cell budding, a strawberry plant sending out a runner, a plant grown from a cutting. The offspring get an exact copy of the parent's genes. Two parents: each parent passes on half of its genes (one of each pair), so the offspring get a new mix and vary.

blocks.name: bi-classify

cards.text: A bacterium divides into two cells
A yeast cell grows a bud that breaks off
A strawberry runner roots and grows a new plant
A potato piece with an eye sprouts
Apple seeds from a flower pollinated by another tree
Kittens in a litter, each a little different

blocks.cap: One parent or two?

blocks.html: Genes come in pairs, one of each pair from each parent. A parent with two different versions of a gene can pass on either one, with equal chances. Each offspring gets its own random pick from each parent, for thousands of genes at once. So brothers and sisters share many genes but almost never the same set.

blocks.name: bi-punnett
blocks.cap: Two black parents, each carrying a brown version, can have black or brown offspring.

blocks.title: Copy or mix?
blocks.q: A gardener wants new plants exactly like her prize-winning rose. Should she plant its seeds or root cuttings?
steps: Seeds come from pollination, so they get genes from two parents: a new mix.
A cutting is a piece of the plant itself: one parent, the same genes.

blocks.title: Trade-offs
blocks.q: Why might a population with two-parent offspring do better when a new disease arrives?
steps: Copies all share the same genes, so a disease that harms one can harm all.
Mixed offspring vary; some may resist the disease.
blocks.a: Variation makes it more likely that some survive.

blocks.html: Students think offspring of two parents get a blend of every trait, like mixing paint. Each parent passes on one of each pair of genes, and the genes stay whole. That is why siblings can differ from each other, and why a trait hidden in both parents can show up in a child.

blocks.html: In One Parent or Two: Copies and Mixes you saw that genes come in pairs, one from each parent. Now meet the versions of a gene, and the reason a trait can skip a generation.

A gene can come in different versions called alleles. You have two alleles for each gene, one from each parent. A dominant allele (written with a capital letter, like P) shows its trait even with one copy. A recessive allele (lowercase, p) shows only when there are two copies.

Gregor Mendel worked this out with pea plants in a monastery garden in what is now the Czech Republic, and published his results in 1866. Crossing purple-flowered and white-flowered plants gave all purple offspring; the white came back in the next generation.

blocks.name: bi-punnett
blocks.cap: Two purple Pp plants: three boxes out of four have at least one P.

blocks.html: Often the dominant allele makes a working protein, such as an enzyme that makes purple pigment, and the recessive allele makes none. One working copy makes enough pigment, so Pp is purple. Only pp, with no working copy, is white. That is how two purple parents, each carrying a hidden p, can have a white-flowered offspring.

blocks.title: Which shows?
blocks.q: In peas, round seeds (R) are dominant over wrinkled seeds (r). What do seeds with Rr look like?
steps: Rr has one dominant allele.
One copy of a dominant allele is enough to show.

blocks.title: Hidden allele
blocks.q: Two black guinea pigs have a white pup. White (b) is recessive. What alleles must each parent carry?
steps: A white pup is bb: one b from each parent.
Both parents are black, so each also has a B.

blocks.html: Students think dominant alleles are the most common, or the "stronger, better" version. Dominant only means the trait shows with one copy. Some dominant alleles are rare: extra toes in cats come from a dominant allele, yet most cats have the usual number.

blocks.html: With Alleles: Dominant and Recessive come two words that save a lot of explaining: one for the letters and one for the look.
The genotype is the pair of alleles (TT, Tt or tt). The phenotype is the trait that shows (tall or short). Two alleles alike (TT or tt) is homozygous; two different (Tt) is heterozygous.

head: Genotype
Name
Phenotype (T = tall dominant)
blocks.cap: Three genotypes, two phenotypes.

blocks.html: Because one dominant allele is enough to show the trait, TT and Tt look the same. The phenotype alone does not tell you which genotype a tall plant has. A short plant is different: it must be tt, since any T would make it tall. So the recessive phenotype always tells you the genotype.

blocks.name: bi-punnett
blocks.cap: A test cross: a tall plant crossed with a short one. If any offspring are short, the tall parent was Tt.

blocks.title: Name them
blocks.q: In pea plants, yellow seeds (Y) are dominant over green (y). Give the genotype name and phenotype of Yy and yy.
steps: Yy: two different alleles, heterozygous; one Y, so yellow.
yy: two alike, homozygous recessive; green.
blocks.a: Yy: heterozygous, yellow. yy: homozygous recessive, green.

blocks.title: Tall: which one?
blocks.q: A tall pea plant is crossed with a short one. Half the offspring are short. What was the tall plant's genotype?
steps: Short offspring are tt, so they got a t from each parent.
The tall parent must have had a t to give: Tt.

blocks.html: Students think TT and Tt must look different, or write a phenotype as letters ("the plant is Tt"). Letters are the genotype. Describe the phenotype in words (tall, purple, round). With complete dominance, TT and Tt have the same phenotype.

sources.name: OpenStax, Concepts of Biology, 8.2 Laws of Inheritance (genotype and phenotype; the test cross)

blocks.html: A Punnett square is a small table that lists every way the parents' alleles can combine. It uses genotypes and turns a cross into something you can count.

Write one parent's two alleles across the top and the other parent's two alleles down the side. Fill each box with one allele from the top and one from the side. The four boxes are the possible genotypes of an offspring.

blocks.name: bi-punnett
blocks.cap: Fill it in: tap each box to choose its genotype, then Check.

blocks.html: Each parent passes on one allele of the pair, and each of the two is equally likely. Listing the two from each parent and pairing them every possible way gives four equally likely combinations. The square is just a tidy way to make sure none is missed or counted twice.

blocks.title: Tt × Tt
blocks.q: Cross two tall pea plants, Tt and Tt. List the boxes.
steps: Top: T, t. Side: T, t.
Row T: TT, Tt. Row t: Tt, tt.
Genotypes: 1 TT, 2 Tt, 1 tt.
Phenotypes: TT and Tt are tall (3 boxes); tt is short (1 box).
blocks.a: 1 TT : 2 Tt : 1 tt, so 3 tall : 1 short.

blocks.title: Bb × bb
blocks.q: A black guinea pig, Bb, is crossed with a white one, bb. What can the offspring be?
steps: Top: b, b. Side: B, b.
Row B: Bb, Bb. Row b: bb, bb.
blocks.a: 2 Bb (black) : 2 bb (white), so half black and half white.

blocks.html: Two mistakes are common. Some students put both of a parent's alleles in one box, like "TTt". Others combine two letters from the same parent. Each box gets exactly two letters: one from the top, one from the side. Check that every box has one letter from each parent.

blocks.html: Each box of a Punnett square is one equally likely outcome. That turns genetics into the theoretical probability you know from math class.
Chance of a genotype or phenotype = (number of boxes with it) ÷ 4. One box out of four is 1/4, or 25%; three boxes is 3/4, or 75%. The chance applies to each offspring separately.

Each offspring is a new, independent draw, like a new roll of a die. A 1/4 chance of a white-flowered plant does not mean one plant in every four will be white. In a small family or litter the count can easily differ from the ratio. With hundreds of offspring, the share gets close to 25%. Mendel counted thousands of pea plants for this reason.

blocks.name: bi-chart

opts.xlabel: Purple-flowered plants out of 4 (each has a 3/4 chance)
opts.title: Pp × Pp: groups of 4 offspring

blocks.cap: Only about 42% of groups of four show exactly 3 purple and 1 white.

blocks.title: Read the chance
blocks.q: Two Pp plants are crossed. What is the chance that one offspring has white flowers (pp)?
steps: The square has PP, Pp, Pp, pp.
Boxes with pp: 1 of 4.

blocks.title: Expected count
blocks.q: From the same cross, a gardener grows 200 seeds. About how many plants will have purple flowers?
steps: Purple boxes: PP, Pp, Pp = 3 of 4.
blocks.a: About 150 (the real count will be near 150, not exactly).

blocks.title: Each one is new
blocks.q: Two Bb guinea pigs have had three black pups. What is the chance the fourth is white?
steps: Each pup is a new draw from the same square.
White (bb) is 1 box of 4. Past pups do not change it.

blocks.html: Students think a 3:1 ratio means exactly 3 of every 4 offspring will show the trait, or that after three black pups a white one is "due." Each offspring is a new chance. Ratios describe what to expect on average over many offspring.

blocks.html: Copying billions of DNA bases is not perfect. In Genes Make Proteins, Proteins Make Traits you saw that a gene's bases set a protein's amino acids. So what happens when a base changes?
A mutation is a change in DNA. It can be harmful, helpful or neutral (no effect), depending on how it changes the protein and on the environment the organism lives in.

blocks.name: bi-central
blocks.cap: One base changes (UUU to UUA), and one amino acid changes: Phe becomes Leu.

blocks.html: There are 64 codons but only 20 amino acids, so many amino acids have several codons. A change from UUU to UUC still gives Phe: the protein is the same, so the mutation has no effect. A change that swaps an amino acid may change the protein's shape a little or a lot. A change that makes a stop codon cuts the protein short. Most mutations land in DNA that does not code for proteins, or change nothing important.

blocks.title: Same or different?
blocks.q: A codon GGC (Gly) mutates to GGA. Use the codon table. Does the protein change?
steps: Look up GGA: Gly.
Gly is still Gly.
blocks.a: No. It is a silent mutation.

blocks.title: A helpful one
blocks.q: Most mammals stop making lactase, the enzyme that digests milk sugar, after they are weaned. Many adults keep making it. How?
steps: A change near the lactase gene keeps the gene switched on into adulthood.
In places where people kept dairy animals, adults with this change could use milk as food.
blocks.a: A mutation that keeps the lactase gene on, which helped where milk was a food.

blocks.html: Students think all mutations are harmful and create monsters. Most have little or no effect, a few are harmful, and some are helpful, like the change that lets many adults digest milk sugar. Whether a mutation helps can depend on the environment.

blocks.html: People have shaped the genes of plants and animals for thousands of years, using what you learned in Punnett Squares and Mutations long before anyone knew about DNA.

In selective breeding, people choose which plants or animals become parents, generation after generation, so a wanted trait becomes more common. It works with variation already in the population. In genetic engineering, scientists move a specific gene into another organism, which then makes that gene's protein.

blocks.name: bi-classify

cards.text: Farmers save seeds from the corn plants with the biggest ears
The human insulin gene is put into bacteria, which make insulin
Breeders pair the gentlest dogs, generation after generation
A gene for resisting an insect pest is moved into a crop plant
Growers pick wild cabbage plants with the biggest flower buds, which over time gave broccoli

blocks.cap: Which method is it?

blocks.html: Selective breeding uses natural variation: some corn plants have bigger ears because of the alleles they carry. Choose those as parents and their alleles become more common in the next generation. It cannot add a gene the population does not have. Genetic engineering can, because it moves DNA itself. The genetic code is the same in nearly all living things, so bacteria can read a human gene and build the human protein.

blocks.title: One plant, many vegetables
blocks.q: Broccoli, cabbage, kale, cauliflower and Brussels sprouts are all one species, Brassica oleracea. How?
steps: Wild cabbage varies: some plants have bigger leaves, some bigger buds, some thicker stems.
Over many generations, growers in different places chose different traits.
No new genes were needed; choosing among existing variation changed each line.
blocks.a: Selective breeding for different traits from the same wild plant.

blocks.title: Insulin from bacteria
blocks.q: In 1982, the FDA approved the first human insulin made by genetically engineered bacteria. Why use bacteria?
steps: Bacteria multiply quickly and are easy to grow in large tanks.
With the human insulin gene inserted, each cell makes the human protein.
blocks.a: They are fast, cheap protein factories once they carry the human gene.

blocks.html: Students think selective breeding creates new genes. It only changes how common existing alleles are. New alleles come from mutations; moving a specific gene from another species is genetic engineering.
People weigh the uses of genetic engineering in food and farming differently. The science above is well established; how and where to use it is a choice communities discuss.

blocks.html: In Earth Science you learned how fossils form and how superposition puts rock layers in order. Put the two together and the rocks become a record of life over time.

In undisturbed rock layers, the oldest layers are at the bottom. The fossils in them, from bottom to top, show that life has changed over Earth's history: many species lived for a time and went extinct, simpler forms appear before more complex ones, and new groups appear in the same order all over the world.

blocks.name: lifesci-strata
blocks.cap: A simplified column of rock layers. Tap a layer to compare its age with the others.

blocks.html: Sediment settles on top of what is already there, so each layer is younger than the one below it. If life had always been the same, we would find the same fossils in every layer. Instead, trilobites appear in old layers and are missing from all the young ones: they died out about 252 million years ago. Mammal fossils appear only in younger layers. And fossils with mixed features show up between the groups they link.

blocks.title: Which is older?
blocks.q: Fossil X is in a layer 30 m deep. Fossil Y is in a layer 5 m deep in the same undisturbed cliff. Which lived first?
steps: Deeper layers formed first (superposition).
X is deeper.

blocks.title: A fossil in between
blocks.q: Tiktaalik, found in 2004 in Arctic Canada in rocks about 375 million years old, has fish scales and fins, but also a neck and sturdy fin bones like simple limbs. Why does it matter?
steps: Older layers have fish but no four-limbed animals.
Younger layers have four-limbed animals.
Tiktaalik, from between them in time, has features of both.
blocks.a: It is a transitional fossil linking fish and four-limbed animals, found where the record predicted.

blocks.html: Students think the fossil record is a complete list of every species, or that all life appeared at once. Fossils form only in special conditions (quick burial, hard parts), so most living things never fossilized and the record has gaps. But the order it shows is the same worldwide, and new finds keep fitting it.

blocks.html: The The Fossil Record shows change over time. Living animals hold clues too. Compare the skeletons of the Vertebrate Groups and a pattern jumps out.

Homologous structures have the same basic bones in the same arrangement, even when they do different jobs, like the arm of a person, the leg of a cat, the flipper of a whale and the wing of a bat. They are evidence that these animals share a common ancestor.

blocks.name: lifesci-limbs
blocks.cap: Same bones, different jobs. Tap a color to find that bone in every limb.

blocks.html: If each limb were designed from scratch for its job, a flipper, a wing and a grasping arm would have no reason to share bones. They do: one upper arm bone, two forearm bones, wrist bones, then finger bones. That is what we expect if they were all inherited from one ancestor with that bone plan, and changed over many generations as the descendants took up swimming, flying or grasping.

blocks.title: Homologous or not?
blocks.q: A bird's wing and a butterfly's wing both do the same job. Are they homologous?
steps: A bird wing has the upper arm, forearm, wrist and finger bones of other vertebrates.
An insect wing has no bones at all: it is a thin sheet of exoskeleton with veins.
They do the same job but are built differently.
blocks.a: No. They are analogous structures: similar jobs that evolved separately.

blocks.name: lifesci-limbs
blocks.cap: A bird wing has bones; an insect wing has none. Same job, different build.

blocks.title: A leftover
blocks.q: Whales have no back legs, yet many have small hip and leg bones buried in their bodies. What does this suggest?
steps: The bones are reduced and do not work as legs.
Their land-living ancestors had back legs.
blocks.a: Whales descend from four-legged ancestors; the bones are vestigial structures.

blocks.html: Students think structures that do the same job, like a bird's wing and a butterfly's wing, show close kinship. Similar jobs can evolve separately. The clue to shared ancestry is shared inner structure, not shared function. Check the bones, not the job.

blocks.html: In 1859, Charles Darwin published On the Origin of Species (Alfred Russel Wallace had reached the same idea on his own), explaining how populations change by natural selection. It joins what you know about adaptations and Alleles: Dominant and Recessive.

Natural selection needs four things: (1) variation: individuals differ; (2) inheritance: some of those differences are passed on in genes; (3) more young than can survive, so there is competition; (4) selection: individuals with helpful traits survive and reproduce more, so those traits become more common over generations.

blocks.name: bi-selection
blocks.cap: Beetles on dark soil. Birds catch the ones they can see. Press Next generation a few times and watch the average color.

blocks.html: Nothing in the process needs a beetle to try to change. Each beetle is born with its color. Light beetles on dark soil are spotted and eaten more often, so fewer of them survive to have young. Dark beetles leave more offspring, and the offspring inherit dark color. Repeat over many generations and the population becomes mostly dark. The individuals did not change; the mix of the population did.

blocks.title: Spot the four parts
blocks.q: A field mouse population has fur from tan to dark brown. Fur color is inherited. Owls hunt at night over pale sand, and each year many more mice are born than survive. What happens?
steps: Variation: tan to dark brown fur.
Inheritance: fur color is passed on.
Too many young: not all survive.
Selection: owls spot dark mice on pale sand more easily, so tan mice survive and reproduce more.
blocks.a: Over generations, tan fur becomes more common.

blocks.name: bi-selection
blocks.cap: Be the bird: tap the beetles you can see, then press Next generation.

blocks.html: Students think individuals change their traits because they need to, like a giraffe stretching its neck and passing on a longer one. Stretching is an acquired trait and is not inherited. Individuals do not evolve; populations do, as inherited traits that help survival become more common.

blocks.html: Natural selection is not only a story about the past. Scientists have measured it happening, by counting how common a trait is generation after generation. This builds on Natural Selection and How Bacteria Multiply.

When the environment changes, the traits that help survival can change too, and data show the population shifting. Two well-studied cases: the peppered moth in England and antibiotic-resistant bacteria.

Peppered moths. Most peppered moths were pale and speckled, hidden on pale, lichen-covered tree bark. The first dark one on record was caught near Manchester in 1848. As coal smoke blackened trees, dark moths were harder for birds to spot, and by 1895 about 98% of the moths caught near Manchester were dark. After clean-air laws such as the Clean Air Act of 1956 cut the soot, the pale form became common again.

blocks.name: bi-chart

opts.title: Dark moths after the air got cleaner (made-up numbers for practice)

blocks.cap: A falling line: as soot decreased, dark moths became less common.

blocks.html: Every step is natural selection. Moths already varied in color (variation), and color is inherited. Birds ate the moths they could see (selection). In each generation, the better-hidden color left more offspring, so it became more common. When the trees changed, the "better" color changed with them.

blocks.title: Resistance
blocks.q: A patient's infection has a few bacteria that happen to resist an antibiotic. What happens when the antibiotic is used?
steps: The antibiotic kills the bacteria that lack resistance.
The resistant few survive and multiply, doubling quickly.
Soon most of the population is resistant.

blocks.q: Using the graph, how much did the share of dark moths fall from 1970 to 1990?

blocks.html: Students think antibiotics cause bacteria to become resistant, the way exercise causes muscles to grow. Resistance comes from mutations that some bacteria already have. The antibiotic kills the others, and the resistant ones survive and multiply.
